Babylon became important under Nimrod (Genesis 10:10) and later in biblical history (see 2 Kings 25:1–30). Its role as a center of pride and idol worship makes it a symbol for the forces opposed to God in the end times (for example, Revelation 14:8; Revelation 16:19; Revelation 18:2). 

• The tower builders gathered together in one place to reach up into God’s realm (God’s dwelling place; Genesis 11:3–4). God came down and scattered them across the earth. In this way, he stopped their idolatrous ambition (their desire to act against him and seek their own glory).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• This account of Shem continues from Genesis 10:21–32, focusing on the family line leading to Abram. Only Abram and Israel inherit Shem’s God (see Genesis 9:26–27; Deuteronomy 32:8–9). The Babel story strongly rejects the culture that God called Abram to abandon (Genesis 12:1; Genesis 24:6–7). Together with the account of Terah’s descendants (Genesis 11:27–32), this account of Shem’s line forms a bridge from the universal history of chapters Genesis 1:1–11 to Israel's national history that begins in chapter Genesis 12:12. 

Abram was part of the small group that remained faithful after the confusion at Babel.

God chose Abram as an act of grace. Through Abram, God began a new plan. God’s purpose was to bless the whole world, even though the nations had been divided and scattered at Babel (Genesis 12:3). 

• the father of (or the ancestor of): Hebrew family records (genealogies, or lists of ancestors) do not always include every generation.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Peleg: See the study note on 10:25.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Nahor was Laban's grandfather. Laban's daughters later married Jacob (chapters Genesis 29:29–31). 

• Lot: See the “Lot” Profile.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: This brief section provides a complete summary of Terah’s life and accounts for his other sons and their marriages. It also introduces Lot, Abram’s nephew, who later played an important role. The ancestors, including Terah and his family, were idolatrous, worshiping other gods in Mesopotamia (Joshua 24:2).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
This is the account: The Hebrew word is toledoth (a term that introduces a new section or family history; see study note on 2:4). This section tells about Terah’s family. 

The details in Genesis 11:28–25:11 are about the family line that comes from Terah. The focus is on Abraham and God’s covenant with him.

The passage also highlights Isaac, the promised child. Isaac continued the family line and carried God’s blessing to the next generation.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Abram received his calling from God in Ur of the Chaldeans (Genesis 15:7; Acts 7:2–4). This was the main city of Sumer in Mesopotamia near the Persian Gulf. The family had moved there perhaps generations before this calling. Their original home ("country," Genesis 12:1) was probably near Haran, in the region of Shem's descendants (Genesis 11:10–26). They settled in Haran after leaving Ur (Genesis 11:31). Later, they were described as Arameans (Deuteronomy 26:5). 

• native land: The same Hebrew phrase appears in Genesis 12:1 ("country"), indicating that Ur, not Haran, was where Abram received his calling (see Genesis 15:7; Nehemiah 9:7; Acts 7:2).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Sarai means "princess" in Hebrew. The text does not mention Sarai's parents. This might have been to create suspense in the story of Abimelech. This story reveals her as Abram's half-sister (Genesis 20:9–12). Later, the law forbade such marriages (Leviticus 18:9; Leviticus 20:17; Deuteronomy 27:22). 

• Nahor's wife was Milcah, who was the daughter of Haran and Nahor's niece (see Genesis 11:29). Her son Bethuel was Rebekah's father. Rebekah became the wife of Abram's son Isaac (Genesis 24:10, Genesis 24:15, Genesis 24:24). The name Milcah is related to the Hebrew word for "queen." 

In Akkadian, it is a title for the goddess Ishtar, the daughter of the moon god. Terah's name is related to the Hebrew word for "moon." His family probably worshiped Sin, the moon god (see Joshua 24:14).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
Sarai, Rebekah, and Rachel could not have children at first (Genesis 25:21; Genesis 29:31). Sarai’s case especially shows the tension between what people could see and what God had promised. God had promised to make Abram into a great nation (Genesis 12:2). 

Israel began through women who could not bear children. This shows that Israel existed because of God’s power and choice. God gave children to women who were barren (unable to have children), as these passages also show (see also 1 Samuel 1:2; 1 Samuel 2:5; Psalm 113:9; Isaiah 54:1).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Terah took: Abram left Ur because God called him (see study note on 11:28). Yet, the story relates from Terah’s viewpoint, reflecting the ancient Near Eastern culture where the oldest male led the family. This respect for elders is probably why Abram did not go to Canaan alone at that time (see Acts 7:2–4). 

• Haran was 885 kilometers (550 miles) northwest of Ur, near the Syrian-Turkish border. Despite the similar name, there is no connection to Terah’s son Haran, who died in Ur (Genesis 11:28).

• Haran means “caravan.” It was a major trade center where ancient trade routes met. 

• Haran was also famous for moon worship, which Terah’s family probably practiced (see study note on 11:29).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Abram knew that he should leave, but he did not know where he was going. Obedience required faith.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: These verses are structured around two commands to Abram: Leave and be a blessing (see study note on 12:2). Each command is followed by three promises conditioned upon obedience.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Through Abram's faith and family, God started to restore the blessing. God called Abram from a pagan world to start a new nation. His promises to Abram later became a covenant (chapter Genesis 15:15). 

• God's calling of Abram later helped convince the Israelites to leave Egypt and go to the land God promised to Abram. It also reminded the Babylonian exiles of their need to return to their own land (for example, Isaiah 51).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• make your name great: Abram gained the fame that the builders of the tower of Babel wanted for themselves (see Genesis 11:4 and study note). 

• so that you will be a blessing: This statement is a command and a promise in Hebrew. It depends on Abram obeying God's command (Genesis 12:1–3): “Go … so that you will be a blessing. I will bless those who bless you and curse those who curse you.”

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Because Abram obeyed the command to be a blessing (Genesis 12:2), God gave him three more promises. 

• those who curse you: People who ignored Abram and his covenant were rejecting God's choice and plan. 

• all the families on earth will be blessed: By faith, they could join the covenant God was making with Abram. The blessing spread worldwide through Abraham, Israel, the covenants, the prophets, Scripture, and the Messiah (Galatians 3:8, Galatians 3:16; compare Romans 9:4–5).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Abram was middle-aged, settled, wealthy, and of high social status. He worshiped many gods (see study note on 11:27–32). When the Lord spoke to him (Genesis 12:1–3), he obediently left his old ways in Ur to follow God's plan. Because Abram responded in faith, God could confirm his promises (Genesis 12:2–3) in a binding covenant (Genesis 15:8–21).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Abram obeyed God's calling and followed his commands (see study note on 12:1–3). He traveled to Canaan (Genesis 12:4–6) and became a blessing (Genesis 12:5–9).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The people (Hebrew hannepesh, meaning "the lives") he brought into his household were probably converts. Abram first became a blessing by influencing his household to follow the Lord.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• the Oak of Moreh: This was probably a Canaanite shrine. Fertile groves were sacred to the Canaanites (compare Isaiah 1:29), and Moreh means "teacher." 

Abram proclaimed the Lord's name beside a pagan place of worship and instruction (Genesis 12:8). 

• Abram continued to be a blessing by building an altar to worship God at Shechem and east of Bethel (Genesis 12:8).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• the LORD appeared to Abram at Shechem (Genesis 12:6) to confirm that this was the promised land. Israel was meant to live in this land, but they needed faith to share in God's promises (compare Numbers 14; Joshua 1:6–9). 

• to your offspring: Abram did not own the land yet. He lived there as a temporary settler.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: he called on the name of the LORD: Calling on the name (identity and character) of the Lord is central to worship and witness (compare Genesis 4:26; see Exodus 34:5–7). Abram needed to distinguish his sacrificial worship from that of the pagan Canaanites.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Abram had to keep moving camp because the Canaanites had the fertile land.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The Nile River supplied plenty of water for crops, so Egypt was usually the last area to experience famine.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Abram's scheme came from fear, putting his family and God's promises at risk. He lacked faith when he went to Egypt. He stopped building altars, and deception became the main pattern of his behavior. Deception would trouble his family throughout Genesis (Genesis 26:1–11; Genesis 27:1–29; Genesis 29:15–30; Genesis 30:34–36; Genesis 31:6–11; Genesis 37:18–35; Genesis 39:7–20). 

• Abram's plan probably followed a custom where a brother arranged his sister's marriage (compare Genesis 24:29–61). Abram may have thought that any possible suitor would have to deal with him, giving him time to leave with Sarai. He did not expect Pharaoh to act without negotiation (Genesis 12:14–16).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• This story shows that God would allow Abram to put his promises at risk in this episode. Soon after Abram obeyed God’s call, a famine tested his weak faith. God rescued Abram and his family, even though Abram acted foolishly. In Egypt, he used deception instead of trusting God to protect him.

• This story intentionally mirrors Israel's later slavery in Egypt:

• Because of a famine (compare Genesis 12:10 with Genesis 47:13), Abram and Israel went to Egypt (compare Genesis 12:10 with Genesis 47:27). 

• There was an attempt to kill the males and save the females (compare Genesis 12:12 with Exodus 1:22). 

• God sent plagues to Egypt (compare Genesis 12:17 with Exodus 7:14–11:10). 

• Abram and Israel took riches from Egypt (compare Genesis 12:16 with Exodus 12:35–36). 

• Pharaoh expelled them (Hebrew shalakh, meaning “send”; compare Genesis 12:19–20 with Exodus 12:31–33) and they went to the Negev (compare Genesis 13:1 with Numbers 13:17, Numbers 13:22). 

Israel was to believe that God would deliver them from bondage in Egypt through the plagues because their ancestor had already been rescued from bondage in Egypt.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Please say you are my sister: This request appears three times in Genesis (see also Genesis 20:2; Genesis 26:7). The text explains that this was Abram’s usual strategy (Genesis 20:13), and his son Isaac did the same thing. The first time this happened was outside the land, and the second time within it (chapter Genesis 20:20). This shows that God protected his promise in both regions.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
Sarai was 65, but she would live to 127. If the biblical lifespans here are understood literally, she had lived only about half her life. By those standards, she may still have been at an age of full strength and maturity.

Sarai and Abram came from a noble family (see study note on 11:29), so she likely had a regal appearance and wore fine clothing. Pharaoh was drawn to both her beauty and the political advantage of an alliance with her family.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Abram was bound by the king’s gift to an unwanted agreement about Sarai that he did not want and could not stop. His plan had put him in a dangerous situation. It put Abram, Sarai, and the promise at risk.

• Abram seemed to gain wealth from his deception, but these new possessions also led to new problems. Abram and Lot had to separate (chapter Genesis 13:13). Hagar, an Egyptian servant, later became the mother of Ishmael’s descendants (chapter Genesis 16:16). In the Bible, these descendants are often shown as being in conflict with Israel.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Pharaoh was a title for a ruler, not a personal name (Genesis 37:36; Exodus 1:15).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: God intervened to rescue Sarai and to preserve her marriage to Abram so that the covenant promise could be fulfilled. When Sarai was returned to Abram, Pharaoh rebuked him because of what had happened (Genesis 12:18–19).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Abram did not need to answer Pharaoh’s questions (Genesis 12:18–19) because Pharaoh’s rebuke was followed by expulsion. Pharaoh’s command echoed God’s command to Abram (Genesis 12:1), but Pharaoh’s words brought Abram shame and disgrace. Even so, God remained faithful and preserved his promise.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: This story takes place during a time of conflict and God's blessings. At the beginning, Abram returns to a place where he had built an altar. The story emphasizes earlier events as Abram returns to the land (Genesis 13:3–4). Abram renews his worship and again calls on the Lord's name (see Genesis 12:8).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Abram already had powerful resources (Genesis 12:5). His time in Egypt increased his wealth and power (Genesis 12:16).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Lot was also wealthy, owning many animals. Tents play an important role in Lot's story (Genesis 13:12). 

• The Canaanites and the Perizzites (see Genesis 34:30; Deuteronomy 7:1; Judges 1:4; Judges 3:5) controlled the fertile land. The argument between Abram's and Lot's herdsmen made Abram easier to attack.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Abram wanted to avoid conflict (Hebrew meribah) because they were close relatives (literally brothers). Later, Moses rebuked Israel for the incident in the wilderness at Meribah (Exodus 17:1–7; Numbers 20:1–13). He taught them to have faith in such situations. So, Meribah became a word of warning for testing and arguing with the Lord in unbelief (see Psalm 95).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: God promised the land to Abram. Abram might have told Lot to find his own place. Abram’s generosity showed his faith. He believed that even if he gave all the land away, God would still provide it to him and his descendants. Abram did not need to hold to things, while Lot's choices were selfish.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• What attracted Lot would not last. In the garden of the Lord, Adam and Eve gave in to their desire for what they saw. Later, Israel became enslaved in Egypt. Sodom and Gomorrah warn us about putting strong desires ahead of obedience to God (Genesis 3:5–6; see 1 John 2:16). 

• Zoar was a small town in the plain where Lot and his daughters later fled (Genesis 19:18–22). Earlier, it was called Bela (Genesis 14:2).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Lot's choice was completely selfish, showing no concern for Abram or faith in the Lord. 

• the whole plain of the Jordan (literally the circle of the Jordan): This was probably near the southern end of the Dead Sea, based on descriptions in ancient records that locate cities of the plain. This area is now very desolate.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The narrator makes many contrasts between Lot and Abram.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: This suggests that Lot would not oppose Sodom's influence because he was focusing on his own interests.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Abram could give Lot the choice land because he believed in God’s promise. Abram waited for God to give him the land. Lot just took what he wanted.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Hebron was an Anakite city (Numbers 13:22) originally called Kiriath-arba (meaning “city of Arba”). It was located in the forested highlands just north of the Negev (Genesis 12:9; Joshua 17:15). Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob all settled there (Genesis 18:1; Genesis 35:27; Genesis 37:14). Sarah, Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob, and Leah were buried in Hebron (Genesis 23:19; Genesis 35:27–29; Genesis 49:29–32; Genesis 50:13). 

• Mamre was an Amorite (Genesis 14:13; Genesis 15:16).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Tidal apparently ruled several city-states. The text calls his people Goiim, which means “nations” in Hebrew.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Archaeology has not identified these kings. But ancient texts include similar names, which supports the report’s reliability. The Mesopotamian kings were allies under one leading ruler, likely Amraphel, who is named first.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: In this typical ancient political conflict, powerful kings allied to control smaller dependent states.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: King Chedorlaomer seems to have defeated the kings of the Siddim Valley earlier and made them pay tribute in asphalt, olive oil, and copper. In the thirteenth year, they stopped paying. In the fourteenth year (Genesis 14:5), the invading kings returned to bring them under their rule again.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: This was Chedorlaomer’s war. Under the feudal system of tribal affiliations, those in covenant with him had to fight. It was also Abram’s battle to rescue Lot, and those under treaty with him had to accompany him.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The invaders came down the King’s Highway on the east side of the Jordan Valley to the Gulf of Aqaba, then circled back to the valley of the Dead Sea.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The five cities of the Plain were close together near the south end of the Dead Sea. The Mesopotamian kings crushed the weak revolt, plundered Sodom and Gomorrah, and carried Lot away with the other captives.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• The word Hebrew appears here for the first time in the Bible. It is different from the later term Habiru found in Egyptian texts. The Habiru were hired soldiers who roamed the land during the time of the judges. 

• Mamre: See study note on 13:18. 

• a brother: Or ally.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Abram … mobilized the 318 trained men born in his household: This shows that Abram was a strong leader and that God’s promise to make him great was already being fulfilled (Genesis 12:2–3). 

• Dan was a city about 241 kilometers (150 miles) north of Abram’s home in Hebron. At that time, the city was called Laish or Leshem (see Joshua 19:47 and study note; Judges 18:29). Dan, the son whose descendants later settled there during the time of the judges, had not yet been born (Genesis 30:6; Judges 18:1–29). It seems that an editor later updated the place name so that later audiences would know which city the text meant.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: God could give his people victory over any forces invading the promised land. Faithfulness to God was necessary for victory. God promises to bless his people and give them victory over the world. He uses those who respond to his call and can skillfully use weapons of war.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Damascus was 64 kilometers (40 miles) north of Dan. Hobah was 97 kilometers (about 60 miles) north of Damascus.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The Valley of Shaveh, or King’s Valley, was probably the Kidron Valley (see 2 Samuel 18:18).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• The name Melchizedek means “king of righteousness.” This suggests the king of Salem was a righteous servant of God. He was probably a Jebusite priest and king. Later writers regarded him as a type of Christ, that is, a person who points forward to Christ (Psalm 110:4; Hebrews 7:1–19). 

• Salem is the ancient name for Jerusalem (compare Psalm 76:2).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: By giving a tenth of everything to Melchizedek, Abram acknowledged Melchizedek as spiritual authority (see Hebrews 7:4). He affirmed that God had given him victory.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Abram understood that accepting the king of Sodom's offer (see study note on 14:1–2) might make him an ally or subject, as Lot had been. This could put God’s promises at risk. Faith looks beyond the world’s riches to the greater blessings that God will give.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: In this oath, Abram may have been making it clear that his God, the LORD (Yahweh), is the same as God Most High, whom Melchizedek spoke about. It is possible that Melchizedek did not know the name Yahweh.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Do not be afraid: Abram did not have a son to inherit his property. The Lord addressed Abram’s anxiety about the future with comforting words.

• I am your shield: The Hebrew word for shield (magen) comes from the same root word as Melchizedek's word delivered (Genesis 14:20). The Lord, who had delivered Abram's enemies into his power, would continue to protect him. 

• your very great reward: The promise of children was still unfulfilled (Genesis 12:2–3; see also Psalm 127:3).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: God made a covenant (a special agreement) with Abram. In this covenant, God confirmed the promises he had made earlier when he summoned Abram to leave his country (Genesis 12:1–3). Abram's descendants would experience a long period of slavery before God made these promises come true.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Abram used wordplay to show his concern that Eliezer of Damascus (Hebrew dammeseq), a man in Abram's household, would become his heir (Hebrew ben-mesheq, which means “son of possession”). This was the usual practice when a man had no son.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: God confirmed that the promise to Abram was for his own children. Then God showed Abram the stars as a sign of the many descendants he would have (Genesis 22:17; Genesis 26:4). The apostle Paul quotes this promise in Romans 4:18 to emphasize Abram’s strong faith.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Abram believed: God made a covenant with someone who trusted in him. The text does not say when Abram first believed. The Hebrew text does not link Abram's belief to the promise about the stars. It simply says that Abram believed the LORD. Abram already had faith. Leaving Ur was his first major act that showed it (see Hebrews 11:8–10). 

• it was credited to him as righteousness: The New Testament quotes this key statement about Abram's faith three times (Romans 4:3; Galatians 3:6; James 2:23). The New Testament writers use this verse to support the teaching that God makes a person right with himself through trust in him (see also Romans 4:22–23).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: In a special ceremony, God made a covenant with Abram and promised to do what he had said.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Obeying God's instructions, Abram collected three herd animals for the ceremony and cut them in half. Cutting the animals symbolized the oath. It showed that the person making the covenant risked his own life if he did not keep his promise (Jeremiah 34:18).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: birds of prey: These are ceremonially unclean birds that symbolize those who unjustly attack Abraham's heirs (Genesis 15:13–14).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• mistreated: The same word appears in Exodus 1:11–12. Egypt, like "birds of prey" (Genesis 15:11), tried to destroy Israel and stop the fulfillment of the covenant. 

• four hundred years: This is probably an approximate number (also Acts 7:6; compare Exodus 12:40; Galatians 3:17). According to the Hebrew text's timeline, the family moved to Egypt around 1876 BC. The exodus happened around 1446 BC, but many scholars believe the Israelites left Egypt later, around 1270 BC (see Exodus Book Introduction, “The Date of the Exodus”).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Not even 400 years of slavery could interfere with God’s plan to fulfill the covenant.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• The reasons for Israel’s bondage included God’s justice. God would tolerate the sins of the Amorites until they fully deserved judgment. 

• is not yet complete: To give the promised land to Israel, God would justly remove those living in the land. Fulfilling promises to Israel also meant judgment for the people in the land. But if they trusted in him, God would save individual people (see Joshua 2:1–15; Joshua 6:23–25; Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25). Until then, God would send Jacob's family to Egypt so Israel could become a great nation. Seeing this future frightened Abram (Genesis 15:12). But it was comforting to know nothing could stop God's plan.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: smoking firepot and a flaming torch: Fire represented the Lord's cleansing and consuming zeal. It also represented how no one could come near him because of his holiness (compare Isaiah 6:3–7). The holy God made (literally cut) a one-sided covenant with Abram. The promises were absolutely certain. This was because they did not rely on what Abram or his descendants' might do.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: God clearly defined the borders of the promised land (the land he promised to give). He told Abram that even though there would be death and suffering, including slavery, he and his descendants would still receive these promises. God confirmed this with an oath (see Hebrews 6:13–14). Nothing can separate God’s people from his love or stop the fulfillment (the bringing about) of his plans (see Romans 8:18–39; 2 Peter 1:3–4).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
Abram and Sarai dealt with the stress of Sarai not being able to have children and being too old to give birth. 

According to the custom in that culture, a woman unable to have children could give her servant as a secondary wife to her husband. The child from this union became the primary wife's child. They adopted the child as the heir. 

Sarai's suggestion was acceptable according to the culture's custom. But it was a human plan that showed a lack of faith in God. God’s promises would be fulfilled by faith.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: While they waited for their promised son to be born, Abram and Sarai tried another plan. This plan did not show trust in God.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Hagar might have thought Abram would favor her instead of Sarai (compare Proverbs 30:21–23).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
the angel of the LORD: The angel of the Lord was the Lord himself in some passages (Genesis 16:13; Genesis 21:17; Genesis 22:11–12; Genesis 31:11–13; Genesis 48:16; Exodus 3:2; Exodus 32:34; Judges 6:11, Judges 6:16, Judges 6:22; Judges 13:22–23; Zechariah 3:1–2). But in other passages he is distinct from the Lord (Genesis 24:7; 2 Samuel 24:16; Zechariah 1:12). 

This figure is often understood as a theophany (a visible appearance of God) or a Christophany (an appearance of the Messiah before he became human (see Genesis 18:1–2; Genesis 19:1; Numbers 22:22; Judges 2:1–4; Judges 5:23; Zechariah 12:8). In these cases, he speaks with the authority of the Lord himself.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
The angel asked Hagar questions that helped her speak openly to God. When she did, God told her to return and submit to Sarai (Genesis 16:9). He also promised that her son would have many descendants, so many that they could not be counted.

The angel of the Lord did not call Hagar Abram’s wife. Instead, he called her Sarai’s servant. Hagar would bear Abram’s child, but Ishmael was not part of God’s covenant with Abram.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
Hagar’s son would become the father of a large nation. This nation would be strong but often hostile, living in the Arabian Desert and frequently in conflict with Israel (compare Genesis 25:18). 

God blessed Ishmael as Abram's descendant. But God did not choose Ishmael to continue the covenant. God kept that blessing for Abram's heir based on God's promise.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Names in Genesis often emphasize the message of a passage. They help the people of God remember the events and their importance in the history of faith. The name Ishmael means "God hears." It marks the moment when the LORD … heard Hagar's cry of distress (see also study note on 16:14–15). This name would have greatly comforted Hagar. God listened to her prayers and acknowledged her complaint.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Hagar showed faith in God through her words and obedience. 

• the God who sees me: God understood Hagar's situation and protected her.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
The name Beer-lahai-roi means “well of the Living One who sees me.” This name and Ishmael were a message and a rebuke for Abram and Sarai (see Genesis 16:11). God notices suffering and listens to those crying out in need. 

Sarai and Abram should have prayed instead of trying to fulfill the promise themselves by following a social custom (compare Genesis 25:21). Giving children to a woman who cannot have them is God's work (Psalm 113:9; compare 1 Samuel 1:1–28; Luke 1:1–25). Humans cannot solve impossible problems. The Lord hears those who suffer, sees their needs, and will provide for them in miraculous ways.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• God Almighty (Hebrew El-Shaddai): This name for God emphasizes his power (see also Genesis 28:3; Genesis 35:11; Genesis 43:14; Genesis 48:3; Genesis 49:25). 

• Walk before Me and be blameless: To bless the nations, Abram needed to obey. Almighty God would guide his actions.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: God gave Abram's family signs that his promises would come true. He changed Abram's name to Abraham (Genesis 17:1–8). He established circumcision as the sign of the covenant (Genesis 17:9–14, Genesis 17:23–27). He changed Sarai's name to Sarah (Genesis 17:15–22).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: God guaranteed his promise by changing Abram’s name. Abram means “exalted father.” This referred to his father Terah and his noble lineage (Genesis 11:27). His new name, Abraham (Hebrew ’ab hamon), means "father of a multitude." This was a wordplay on the promise of his countless descendants (see also John 8:31–59; Romans 4:16–17; Galatians 3:7, Galatians 3:15–19, Galatians 3:29). Whenever the new name was used, he and his household would remember that a multitude of nations would come from him.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: kings will descend from you: This is the first sign that Israel would become a nation ruled by kings (see also Genesis 35:11; Genesis 36:31; Numbers 24:7; Deuteronomy 17:14–18; Deuteronomy 28:36).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The land of Canaan was to be an everlasting possession for the descendants of Abraham. The Lord would always be their God (see Jeremiah 31:31–40; Zechariah 8:8; Luke 1:68–79; Revelation 21:1–4).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: God gave circumcision as a confirming sign that reminded all households of loyalty to the covenant.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
will be cut off: This punishment seems to have several applications. A person could be exiled from society or put to death by the community; most often it warned that a person might die prematurely (see Exodus 31:14; Leviticus 7:20–27; Leviticus 17:3–4; Leviticus 20:17–18; Leviticus 23:28–29; Numbers 15:30–31; see also Psalm 31:22; Ezekiel 21:4; Romans 9:3; Romans 11:22). 

Failure to be circumcised was a serious violation of the covenant (see Exodus 4:24–26; compare Galatians 5:2–4).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Sarah’s new name marked an important step in her calling (God’s purpose for her life). It fit her role as the future mother of kings and pointed to God’s promise.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: he laughed (Hebrew yitskhaq): This was because the promise seemed unbelievable. He thought his family line would continue through Ishmael. But Abraham and Sarah would have their own son.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The name Isaac (Hebrew yitskhaq) means “he laughs.” This recalls Abraham's disbelief when he heard God's promise. It also reminds us of God's favor and pleasure at Isaac's birth (compare Genesis 21:6).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: God would not abandon Ishmael. His family would prosper (see Genesis 25:13–16). But the covenant promises were for Isaac.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: After God spoke to Abraham about Isaac, Abraham followed God's instructions immediately. He performed circumcision as a sign of faith, showing their participation in the covenant (compare Romans 4:11–12; Galatians 5:2–6, Galatians 5:11; Galatians 6:15; Philippians 3:2–3; Colossians 2:11–12; 1 Peter 3:21).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
The Lord's visit to Abraham set the time for Isaac's birth. The three visitors were probably the Lord and two angels (see study note on 16:7). Abraham welcomed the visitors peacefully and generously, which contrasted with the chaos and corruption in Sodom (chapter Genesis 19:19). 

Sharing a meal was important for making or confirming covenants. When God was ready to fulfill the covenant promise, he personally shared a meal with Abraham. Fellowship with God has always included a communal meal (see Exodus 24:9–11; Matthew 26:17–30 // Luke 22:7–38; Acts 2:42; 1 Corinthians 11:20–34).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Abraham received his visitors as very important guests, perhaps realizing that they were messengers from God.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: My lord: The Hebrew text uses ’adonay, which always refers to God. In Hebrew tradition, people said this word when they saw the letters of God's holy name ("Yahweh") in the text. The text here might use ’adonay instead of the more common ’adoni to show this was the angel of the Lord, meaning the Lord himself (see study note on 16:7). We do not know if Abraham knew who his visitors were at first. But by the end of the story, he knew he had been talking with God.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The visitors asked about Sarah by name, even though no one had told them who she was.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: I will surely return: The Hebrew phrase is emphatic. The statement announced a certain promise and dramatic change.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Sarah thought no one noticed her disbelieving laughter. But God knows what people do in secret and what they feel (see Psalm 69:5; Proverbs 20:27; Mark 4:22; Luke 8:43–48; Hebrews 4:13). He knows if they doubt promises or trust in him (see Hebrews 11:11–12).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
Is anything too difficult for the LORD?: This question does not expect an answer. It teaches that nothing is too difficult for God.

God can do great and surprising things. For those who live in covenant (a binding promise relationship) with him, nothing is impossible, because nothing is too hard for the Lord.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: God trusted Abraham as his prophet (Genesis 18:16–21; see Genesis 20:7). In return, Abraham pleaded that God would save Sodom (Genesis 18:23–32; see Hebrews 7:23–26). God can do anything he wants. This passage confirms it will be fair and right.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Abraham was responsible for teaching his descendants to be righteous and act justly so they might enjoy God's blessings. It was important for Abraham to know how God’s righteousness was at work in judgment.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The outcry: See Ezekiel 16:49–50.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: God, who knows everything, was cautious in his judgment. He knew the sins of Sodom and Gomorrah. This careful examination showed God's justice in a way humans could understand. He would not destroy the people unless he was certain they were wicked.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
Abraham probably thought there were more righteous people in Sodom and Gomorrah than there were (see study note on 19:14). Concerned for them, he made a legal appeal to the Lord based on God's justice. His prayer might seem bold, as if he were negotiating with God. But he approached God with true humility and respect. He did not try to convince God to act against his will. Instead, he prayed for the well-being of others (compare with Lot’s prayer, Genesis 19:18–23). 

God is a fair judge. "Righteousness exalts a nation" (Proverbs 14:34). Righteous people help preserve society (compare Matthew 5:13).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• The two angels also first appeared to Abraham as men (Genesis 18:2). 

• Lot was no longer living in tents near Sodom (Genesis 13:12). He had become a citizen and leader in Sodom, sitting at the city entrance. Community leaders (elders) usually gathered at the gates. This is where they publicly finalized legal and business matters (compare Genesis 23:18; Job 29:7, Job 29:12–17). 

As a righteous man, Lot tried to guide the people of Sodom to live better lives (2 Peter 2:7–8; compare Genesis 19:9). While he opposed their evil behavior, Lot still chose Sodom’s wealthy lifestyle over the simpler life in the hills (compare Genesis 13:10–11). Life in the hills offered fewer temptations and less corruption but lacked the comforts of Sodom. 

As long as the Lord left Lot and his family alone in Sodom, he lived comfortably and kept his belief in God. But, he could not continue living this way. Sodom would have destroyed Lot if the Lord had not destroyed Sodom. 

• This story showed Israel that God is the righteous judge of the whole earth (Genesis 18:25). He punishes evil fairly. In evil societies, wrongdoing leads to unfair treatment and suffering for others.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The two angels who were with the Lord at Mamre (compare Genesis 18:2, Genesis 18:22) went on to Sodom. They knew the people there were very wicked. Even though Lot welcomed them, they first chose to stay in the public square instead of going into his house.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
The Canaanites were evil people who tried to corrupt others. God judged their immoral civilization and warned others not to be like them. It was difficult to get Lot and his family out of Sodom. But it was even more difficult to remove Sodom's influence from them. 

This chapter helped later Israelites understand the moral and spiritual dangers of the people living in and around the promised land. This included the Canaanites and Lot’s descendants, the Moabites and the Ammonites (see Numbers 22–25; Deuteronomy 23:3–6; Joshua 24:9; Judges 10:7–9; Judges 11:4–5; 1 Samuel 10:27; 1 Kings 11:1–3; 2 Kings 24:2).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The evil actions of the men of the city were matched by the hypocrisy of Lot (Genesis 19:6–9). The men acted in a wicked and violent way toward Lot’s visitors. Lot tried to protect his guests. However, he offered his daughters to the crowd instead. This action showed serious moral failure.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
Lot strongly opposed the men’s plan to harm his guests. He spoke against their wicked actions. However, he wrongly offered his daughters to protect the visitors, which showed a serious moral failure.

At first, Lot had only set up his tent near Sodom. Over time, he became closely tied to the city, and its influence shaped his life.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The men of the city became enraged because Lot tried to stop their evil behavior. It was amazing to them that Lot would judge them, since he apparently had not done so before.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Lot’s warning words were not taken seriously because of his hypocrisy. It seemed that there would not be even ten righteous people in the city.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Lot escaped God's judgment because of God's grace, but Lot was still hesitant to leave Sodom. Israel would forever remember Lot as someone who hesitated and needed angels to pull him to safety. The Lord was merciful and spared Lot because of Abraham (Genesis 18:23; Genesis 19:29).

• Today, people who follow God often feel pressure to copy the wrong ways that many people live. God asks his followers to live differently from people who do not follow him. This means Christians should choose actions and behaviors that show they belong to God (1 John 2:15–17). God will judge the corrupt systems of the world. This judgment will be even more severe than the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah (Matthew 11:23–24).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Lot asked the angels for permission to live in the small town of Zoar (which means "little place") even after they saved him.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Compare Luke 17:29. The eruption of Mount Vesuvius, the volcano that destroyed Pompeii in AD 79, along with more recent natural disasters, shows how quickly a complete disaster like this can happen.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
looked back: The verb form indicates intense gazing at the world she loved, not just a curious look (Genesis 15:5; Exodus 33:8; Numbers 21:9; 1 Samuel 2:32; compare Exodus 3:6). Lot’s wife had become too attached to Sodom to follow God's calling. So God judged her as she lingered on the valley slopes. 

Christ’s return to judge the world will be as sudden and devastating as Sodom's destruction (Luke 17:32–37). Those who desire the life of this wicked world will lose both this world and the next.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: God listened to Abraham's plea (compare Genesis 18:23–32). But Lot lost everything during the destruction of Sodom. His choice to live in the fertile land of Sodom eventually led him into a dangerous situation (Genesis 13:10–13). After this, he could no longer remain in the land he had chosen.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Sodom's culture apparently influenced Lot’s daughters more than their father's values. They had no issues having children with their drunk father because they saw no other way to continue their family line (see Genesis 9:21–22).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The poverty of the cave contrasts with the wealth Lot shared with Abram and the good life he lived in Sodom. Abraham would father a righteous nation (Genesis 17:1), but Lot and his daughters started a new Sodom.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• The daughters' plan worked. They each became pregnant by their father. From these two sons, born from incest, came two of Israel's long-time enemies: the nations of Moab and Ammon. Their extreme wickedness was partly due to their origins. 

• Both daughters chose descriptive names for their sons. Moab means "from my father" and Ben-ammi means "son of my people." These names subtly hinted at their actions without making people suspicious who were unaware of the stories.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Gerar was near the coast in Philistine land, about 19 kilometers (12 miles) south of Gaza and 80 kilometers (50 miles) southwest of Hebron.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• This second "sister story" in Genesis (compare Genesis 12:10–20) happened just before Sarah became pregnant with Isaac (chapter Genesis 21:21). In both instances, God protected Abraham and Sarah's marriage to keep it pure for the covenant promises. To be part of God's plan, his people must separate from worldly corruption. 

• This story happened in the promised land. It showed Israel how God intervened in people's lives to fulfill his plan. He protected them from threats from other tribes. He used his chosen people to mediate his relationship with other nations. 

• By preventing adultery from destroying Abraham's marriage, God reminded the Israelites not to marry those who would lead them away from the Lord (Ezra 9:1–4; Nehemiah 13:23–27; Malachi 2:10–17). They should not allow any chance for temptation. Adultery would eventually destroy the covenant and the people.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Abraham lied to Abimelech, just as he had lied to Pharaoh (Genesis 12:13). Isaac later did the same (Genesis 26:1–11), probably learning this from his father.

• Abimelech (which means "my father the king") was probably a title like Pharaoh (Genesis 37:36; Exodus 1:15), not a personal name (see study note on Genesis 26:1).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: One night … God came … in a dream: God urgently intervened to stop Abimelech from harming Sarah's purity right before fulfilling his promise (Genesis 18:10; Genesis 21:1–3).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: God gave Abimelech a strong warning against committing adultery. This was a crime that could be punished by death (compare Exodus 20:14). The ancient Near East considered it "tremendous guilt" (Genesis 20:9).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Abimelech was innocent (Genesis 20:6). He knew of no wrong he had done. But he was close to committing adultery. Not knowing the truth does not remove guilt (Leviticus 4:13–14). 

• would You destroy a nation even though it is innocent?: Abimelech's plea to God echoes Abraham's earlier words (compare Genesis 18:23–32). It shows Abraham's lack of faith at this time.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Because Abimelech acted with a clear conscience, God kept him from sinning. God will graciously help those who try to do what is right. When people act with reverence toward God, God gives them more revelation and draws them into more specific faith (see Acts 10).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Abraham's prayer saved the king's life and restored his family (Genesis 20:17–18). Abimelech learned that Abraham's God was sovereign (meaning God has complete power and authority over everything). Abraham, as God's prophet, received God's messages and would pray for others (see Numbers 12:13; Deuteronomy 9:20). This was true even if he did not always act like a prophet.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Abraham received rebukes from Abimelech and God (compare Genesis 12:17–19). Abimelech was upset because Abraham's lie made him guilty of this serious sin (see study note on 20:3–7). Abimelech understood that taking a married woman into his harem (a group of wives and concubines) was wrong.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Abraham's deceit was not just a brief loss of faith. Even after being scolded in Egypt, he used this strategy everywhere he traveled (compare Genesis 12:12–13). Living by faith requires perseverance.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Abimelech showed he was an honorable person by making things right (see study note on 20:4–5). He made things right by letting Abraham live in the area. He also gave him slaves, livestock (compare Genesis 21:27), and 1,000 pieces of silver to make up for any wrong done to Sarah.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The inability to have children suggests that some time had passed. God controls births. He decides when women can have children (Genesis 25:21; Genesis 29:31; Genesis 30:2, Genesis 30:17, Genesis 30:22–23; 1 Samuel 1:19–20; Psalms 113:9; Psalms 127:3; Luke 1:13).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: See Genesis 18:10.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Abraham responded in faith by naming his son Isaac and circumcising him according to the terms of the covenant (see Genesis 17:9–14).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Isaac was born 25 years after God first made the promise to Abraham (compare Genesis 12:4).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Sarah’s made a wordplay with the name Isaac (Hebrew yitskhaq, meaning “he laughs”). It shows how laughing in disbelief turned to laughing in joy when God fulfilled the promise (Genesis 18:12). Isaac’s name might reflect the pleasure of God and his parents at his birth. Sarah knew everyone who heard about this would laugh and celebrate with her.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Sarah was filled with joy and praise for this amazing event. Only God could enable her to have a child.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The feast for Isaac’s weaning probably happened when he was three. Ishmael was around 17 years old at that time (Genesis 16:16). Sarah saw Ishmael mocking her son, Isaac. The verb metsakheq (“mocking”) is related to the word for “laughter.” This theme (Genesis 21:6) becomes negative because of Ishmael’s mocking.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: God used the incident of Ishmael’s mocking Isaac to separate Ishmael and Hagar from the family and the child of promise. They would constantly threaten the promised descendant if they remained with the family.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Earlier, Sarah mistreated Hagar and forced her to flee (Genesis 16:6). Later, when Hagar’s son mistreated Isaac, Sarah insisted that the slave woman and her son leave.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Abraham was upset when Sarah asked him to send Hagar and Ishmael away. God told Abraham to agree, promising that Ishmael would also have a future as Abraham's descendant.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
God rescued Hagar and Ishmael in the wilderness and promised them a future (compare Genesis 16:7–14). This passage is like chapter Genesis 16:16, but there are key differences. God saves Hagar and Ishmael, but there is no special naming. God repeats the promise to Hagar, but she is not told to return to Sarah. 

These repeated themes show God's plan for Hagar and Ishmael. As Joseph later explained to Pharaoh, a repeated event confirms God's plan (Genesis 41:32). God did not leave Hagar and Ishmael alone. He met them in their time of despair (compare Genesis 16:7). He gave them what they needed and promised again that Ishmael would start a great nation (Genesis 21:13; see Genesis 16:11–12). 

Paul uses this story in his letter to the Galatians to show that God’s people must let go of anything that could block God’s promise from being fulfilled (Galatians 4:21–31).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: a bowshot away: This means the distance an arrow can travel when someone shoots a bow. The phrase connects with Ishmael’s future work as an archer (Genesis 21:20).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
Abimelech wanted a treaty so that Abraham would not deceive him. He knew that God was blessing Abraham, even though Abraham had not always been truthful (Genesis 20:9–10). This sad contradiction made the treaty necessary. 

By contrast, God’s people are called to speak truthfully. Paul teaches believers to speak the truth in love (Ephesians 4:15, Ephesians 4:25). Jesus also warned against using oaths to distort the truth (Matthew 5:37; James 5:12).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
At the high point of this passage, it explains the name of Beersheba, where Abraham lived (Genesis 21:31–34). The name is linked to the covenant (a binding agreement) that Abraham made with the people of the land. This agreement allowed him to live there in peace and safety.

In this way, God’s promise was beginning to come true (Genesis 12:7; Genesis 13:14–17; Genesis 15:7, Genesis 15:18–21; Genesis 17:8).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The theme of the well appears again (see Genesis 16:14; Genesis 21:19). God provided water, symbolizing blessing, in the dry wilderness. Later, he even brought water from a rock for Israel (Exodus 15:22–27; Exodus 17:1–7; Numbers 20:1–13).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Abraham gave gifts to Abimelec (compare Genesis 20:14). These gifts helped confirm his legal right to live peacefully in the land and to claim the well as his own. Beersheba marked another step toward the fulfillment (completion) of God’s promise.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
The Philistines mentioned in Genesis are not the same as the Philistines in Judges through Kings. The earlier group had Semitic (ancient Near Eastern) names, such as Abimelech, and they followed Canaanite culture.

The later Philistines were likely from the Aegean region (near Greece). They had different customs and culture. They seem to have come to Canaan by sea around 1200 BC, during the time of the judges.

Because of this, the name Philistines in Genesis is probably used to describe the earlier people of the region in a way that later audiences would understand.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• A tamarisk tree requires a lot of water. Planting it showed Abraham felt secure in his land rights and trusted God to provide water in the desert. Although he was a foreigner, living under the tree represented peaceful security (compare Zechariah 3:10). 

• there he called upon the name of the LORD: See study note on 12:8.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
Some time later: Abraham had sent Ishmael away and settled in the land. Then God tested Abraham’s faith by telling him to give up Isaac. This challenged Abraham's logic and understanding of God. 

Would he still obey when God seemed to oppose him and the covenant? Would he hold onto the boy or surrender him to God (see Exodus 13:11–13)? Did he believe that God would still keep his promise and bless the world through Abraham’s descendants?

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The biggest test in Abraham's life came after he finally had the promised child, Isaac, after waiting a long time. He had grown to love Isaac and enjoyed his company for many years.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Abraham's earlier obedience to God's calling (Genesis 12:1–3) brought him great blessings. Now, he had a chance to show even greater obedience. 

• Take your son ... Isaac, whom you love: God described Isaac in detail to remind Abraham that Isaac was his beloved son, reinforcing the cost of the sacrifice. 

• The name Moriah is explained by the Chronicler (2 Chronicles 3:1) as the future site of the temple mount in Jerusalem. 

• go: God worded the command this way to help Abraham remember his earlier call and obey again (Genesis 12:1–3).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Abraham's immediate and unquestioning obedience is as remarkable as the test itself.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The boy and I will go over there to worship, and then we will return to you: Abraham's amazing statement makes us wonder what he was thinking. Abraham knew that God had planned the future of the covenant around Isaac and that God wanted him to sacrifice Isaac. He could not reconcile these things in his mind; he could only do what God commanded him to do, and leave the future to God (compare Hebrews 11:17–19).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: When Isaac asked, Abraham showed his faith in the Lord by saying, "God Himself will provide." But he did not know how. This idea is central to the entire story.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
God’s intervention was dramatic and instructive, confirming that he never intended for Isaac to be sacrificed. God later made it clear that child sacrifice was an abomination to him (see Leviticus 18:21; Leviticus 20:1–5; Deuteronomy 18:10; 2 Kings 16:2–3; Isaiah 57:5; Jeremiah 32:35). God wanted Abraham to sacrifice his own will and surrender it to God, and when he did, God intervened.

This story sets an example for all who worship through sacrifice. Like Abraham, true worshipers understand that everything belongs to God. They acknowledge that all things come from God and are his. A true worshiper obediently gives God what he asks for. They trust that God will provide all needs. Through this trust, they experience that God always provides.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The angel of the Lord stopped Abraham just as he was ready to plunge the knife into his son.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Now God knew that Abraham would hold nothing back from him, that he did truly fear God. To fear the Lord means to reverence him as sovereign, trust him implicitly, and obey him without protest. The sacrifice that pleases God is a heart broken of self-will, surrendered to God (Psalms 40:6–8; Psalms 51:17). 

• you have not withheld: Compare Romans 8:32, which uses the same verb (“spare”) as the Greek Old Testament here. If God gave us his most precious possession, he will surely provide everything we need.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
God provided a ram caught by its horns in a bush for the sacrifice. God graciously allowed Abraham to substitute an animal sacrifice instead of Isaac. Later, all of Israel would offer animals to the Lord, understanding that God's grace allowed this substitution (Exodus 29:10; Leviticus 4:15; Leviticus 16:20–22). 

In the New Testament, God substituted his only son for all humanity. This perfect sacrifice was made once and for all people (Isaiah 53:6, Isaiah 53:10; John 1:29; Hebrews 10:1–14; Hebrews 7:27; 1 Peter 3:18).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• As in many stories about the patriarchs (early fathers of Israel), the key meaning is preserved through naming. Yahweh-Yireh means "the Lord will provide" (see Genesis 22:8). The use of the divine name Yahweh (the personal name of God) shows that the patriarchs knew this name (compare Exodus 6:2–3), even if they did not yet understand its full meaning (see study note on Exodus 6:2–3). 

• to this day: Later Israelites saw this story as a lesson about their worship in Jerusalem. Abraham's sacrifice happened on the mountain of the Lord, which later became the site of the temple in Jerusalem (see study note on 22:2). Three times a year, the people of Israel brought their best offerings to God for sacrifice. They trusted he would continue to provide for them.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
After the event, God again confirmed his covenant with Abraham (compare Genesis 15:5, Genesis 15:18–21; Genesis 17:3–8). His descendants would be numerous: 

• like the stars in the sky (compare Genesis 26:4), 

• like the sand on the seashore (compare Genesis 32:12), and

• like the dust of the earth (compare Genesis 13:16; Genesis 28:14).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: By Myself: There is no higher name by which God can swear (Hebrews 6:13–17).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Joshua and Old Testament Israel partially fulfilled the promise that Abraham’s descendants would conquer the cities (literally take possession of the gates) of God's enemies. The church will completely fulfill this promise (compare Matthew 16:18 and the study note there).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Abraham proved his faith. Afterward, he needed to pass the covenant blessings to Isaac. He bought a burial plot (chapter Genesis 23:23), found a wife for Isaac (chapter Genesis 24:24), and distributed his property (Genesis 25:1–11).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Milcah was the wife of Nahor. She was also his niece (see Genesis 11:29).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: A report came from the east that Abraham’s brother Nahor (see Genesis 11:27–29) was doing well. The people in the next part of the story are introduced here.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Uz may have been an ancestor of Job (Job 1:1).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Bethuel was the youngest of Nahor’s eight sons with Milcah. He was the father of Rebekah, who would become Isaac’s wife (see Genesis 24:15, Genesis 24:67). Rebekah would succeed Sarah as the clan's female leader (Genesis 23:1–2).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Sarah was 127 years old, and Isaac was 37 at this time (compare Genesis 17:17). 

• Hebron: See the study note on 13:18.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: She died: Abraham bought a piece of land for Sarah's burial. This was the first sign of a permanent change, as people usually buried their dead in their ancestral homeland (compare Genesis 49:29–50:13). By burying Sarah, Abraham separated himself from his ancestral home (where his relatives still lived, Genesis 22:20–24). His future would be in Canaan, where his descendants would fulfill the promise.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Abraham negotiated with local Hittite elders to buy land for a burial site. These Hittites had moved south to Canaan from the large Hittite empire in what is now Turkey (compare Genesis 10:15).

• Abraham was a foreigner and an outsider among them. But he trusted God's promise that he would eventually own the land.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• sir. You are God's chosen one (or prince; Hebrew my lord, you are a lifted up one of God): Either Abraham was well-respected by these people, or they were politely asking for his generosity.

• Bury your dead in the finest: They were ready to fulfill his request, especially if it meant they could legally bind him to themselves (Genesis 23:11).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Abraham wanted to buy Ephron’s cave at Machpelah, but Ephron wanted him to buy the entire field.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: This cave would serve as the permanent burial site for Abraham's family. It was near Mamre (Genesis 23:19), where Abraham lived (see Genesis 13:18; Genesis 14:13; Genesis 18:1). They would bury Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, and Jacob and Leah there (Genesis 23:19; Genesis 25:9; Genesis 35:27–29; Genesis 49:29–31; Genesis 50:13). This marked their lasting presence in the promised land.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Ephron did not intend to give the cave to Abraham for free. He expected Abraham to pay the full price. Ephron wanted to sell the cave to avoid taking care of it and to get the highest price possible.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Abraham did not want the whole field, but he was willing to take it to get the cave.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: four hundred shekels of silver: This was a high price. Ephron's politeness was part of the usual bargaining process.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
Abraham paid the full amount and completed the deal. He avoided debt by not accepting gifts from the people (compare Genesis 14:21–24). The Hittite elders witnessed the deal, ensuring no one could dispute Abraham's ownership of the land. The transaction happened at the city gate, where they conducted public legal and business matters (see Genesis 19:1). 

The land became Abraham's permanent property, a first step toward God's promise to give him the land. God had not yet fulfilled his promise with this purchase. Abraham knew it, so he planned for the future (Genesis 12:7). By buying land for his dead, he showed that God's promises continue beyond this life. This is the hope for all who die with faith.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Trusting in the Lord's promise, Abraham had his main servant promise to find a wife for Isaac (probably Eliezer, Genesis 15:2). Abraham told his servant to return to his relatives in his homeland, 724 kilometers away (about 450 miles). Abraham was faithful to the covenant by planning for Isaac's future.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Isaac's marriage to Rebekah made it certain that God's plan would continue for the next generation. God showed his covenant faithfulness by working through his faithful people (Genesis 24:12, Genesis 24:27, Genesis 24:49).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The servant placed his hand under Abraham's thigh (compare Genesis 47:29). This was the custom when making a serious oath. The servant accepted the responsibility of completing this mission.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Isaac knew how wicked and threatening the local Canaanite people were, so he maintained separation from them (compare Genesis 26:34–35; Genesis 27:46; Genesis 28:8–9).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The servant was never to take Isaac out of the promised land to find a wife. Abraham protected Isaac and made sure God’s promises would remain tied to the land of blessing.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
Aram-naharaim means "Aram of the two rivers." It was also known as Paddan-aram, which means "the field of Aram" (compare Genesis 25:20). 

The journey took two weeks each way. So, the servant took 10 of his master’s camels and departed with all kinds of gifts (Genesis 24:22, Genesis 24:53).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The servant obeyed his master’s instructions and trusted God to lead him to the right woman.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The servant faithfully completed his mission. God showed his faithful covenant love to Abraham's family by bringing all these details together. God was working quietly through these events to carry out his will through people who acted responsibly and in faith.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Abraham’s future daughter-in-law showed hospitality and hard work, similar to Abraham (see Genesis 18:1–8). Ten thirsty camels could drink 946 liters (250 gallons) of water. A woman willing to do that much work for a stranger was certainly not lazy, but generous and hospitable.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The servant received a precise, immediate answer to his prayer for guidance.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The servant thanked the girl by giving her expensive jewelry.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: God guided the servant to Abraham's relatives.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Rebekah again showed kindness by offering lodging for the servant and food for his camels.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The servant bowed to the ground and worshiped the Lord for his loyal love and faithfulness in guiding him to the exact family he sought.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: the LORD, the God of my master Abraham, who has not withheld His kindness and faithfulness from my master: These words express this chapter’s message (compare Genesis 24:48). Believers can trust the Lord’s leading because he is sovereign in all things. He never leaves his people to their own resources in carrying out his covenant work.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Laban … rushed: He did not want to miss the chance to marry off his sister and get more gifts. Laban's reaction to the servant's wealth hints at his greedy nature (see Genesis 24:54–56 and study note; Genesis 29:21–27; Genesis 30:27–36; Genesis 31:1–13).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The servant stayed focused on his mission. He insisted on sharing his story before eating. He explained his mission and recognized God's providence in leading him to Rebekah. He did this before taking care of his own needs. The servant wanted everyone to understand that this was God's work, not a chance or humanly arranged meeting.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The way that God directed this event from behind the scenes is different than in most of Genesis, but it is true to how the life of faith normally works. Faith, expressed in personal prayer and obedience, looks for evidence of God’s working. Believers usually have to make wise choices and remain faithful to the covenant, trusting that God will guide them through the circumstances of life to accomplish his will.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Following his testimony about God’s guidance, the servant secured the family’s blessing and permission to take Rebekah to his master’s son Isaac.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The servant gave expensive gifts to Rebekah, her mother, and her brother to conclude the arrangements.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: It was hard for Rebekah’s family to let her go so suddenly, and Laban may have hoped to gain more wealth. However, the servant had sworn an oath and would not rest until it was completed. There was no reason for him to stay.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
Rebekah chose to leave at once to be with her new husband, which ended the disagreement. She accepted what seemed to be the Lord’s clear leading.

In that culture, young women usually wanted to marry (not marrying brought great shame and hardship). Later stories about Laban help explain why Rebekah may have wanted to leave (compare Genesis 31:14–15). 

Rebekah showed faithful love to the servant, to Abraham’s family, and to Isaac by going to become his wife.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: When Rebekah left, her family blessed her, hoping she would become the mother of millions. They said, May your offspring possess the gates of their enemies. Rebekah's marriage to Isaac was part of God's plan to bless "all the families of the earth" (Genesis 12:1–3).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Isaac lived in the Negev, in the southern part of Canaan.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Isaac was 40 years old when he married Rebekah (Genesis 25:20), so Abraham was 140 (Genesis 21:5).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The exact time when Abraham married Keturah is unknown. It was probably after Sarah's death, but this is not certain.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Even though Abraham had sons with another wife, he protected Isaac's inheritance and blessing.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The birth of these nations from Abraham partially fulfilled God’s promise to him (Genesis 12:2; Genesis 17:4).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Sheba and Dedan: Compare Genesis 10:7. Abraham’s descendants probably settled in these regions. They became known by these names, along with people from other family lines.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Abraham loved all his sons, so before he died, he gave them gifts and sent them away as he had sent Ishmael (Genesis 21:8–14). This made certain that Isaac remained his heir.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: These verses mention Abraham's death before Jacob and Esau are born. But he actually lived until they were 15 years old (Genesis 25:19–26; compare Genesis 21:5; Genesis 25:26). This storytelling choice ends Abraham's story before focusing on Isaac's family.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: God blessed his son Isaac. Abraham had sent his other sons away. Isaac lived near Beer-lahai-roi, a special place where God answered prayers (Genesis 16:14) and where Isaac waited for the Lord (Genesis 24:62).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: This record lists Ishmael’s descendants before giving the details of Isaac’s descendants (see Genesis 25:19–35:29). This follows the literary structure of Genesis (see Genesis Book Introduction, “Summary”).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Ishmael's 12 sons fulfilled God's promise of blessings (Genesis 17:20).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Havilah was a region in north-central Arabia. 

• Shur was an area between Beersheba and Egypt. 

• And they lived in hostility toward all their brothers: This wording is similar to Genesis 16:12.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Isaac … married Rebekah: Isaac’s marriage connected him and his family more closely to Abraham’s relatives. If he had married a Canaanite woman, the faith of the covenant could have been endangered by these corrupt people and their mixed worship.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob’s struggle to be greater than his brother began before the twins were born (see Hosea 12:3).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: This account of the family of Isaac, the chosen son of Abraham, mostly recounts Jacob’s struggle for the blessing (Genesis 25:27–34; chapters Genesis 27:27–33).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• For 20 years, Rebekah could not have children (compare Genesis 25:20, Genesis 25:26), similar to Sarah (see Genesis 16:1). This condition tested their faith (see study note on 16:1–3). How could they be childless when God promised that nations would come from them? 

• Isaac begged the Lord for help, and the Lord answered his prayer. Isaac seemed to learn from his father's mistake and acted with faith.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: When Rebekah’s pregnancy was difficult, she went to ask the LORD about it. She likely did this by visiting a prophet (a person who speaks God’s message), possibly Abraham (Genesis 20:7; see study note on 25:7–8).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• nations: Jacob and Esau fought in the womb, and their descendants (Israel and Edom) fought continuously throughout their history. In their many conflicts, Israel achieved supremacy over Edom.

• the older will serve younger: God chose the younger son over the elder, which went against the usual order (compare Genesis 48:12–14; see Malachi 1:1–3; Romans 9:11–16).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: When the twins were born, the unusual circumstances inspired each boy’s name and hinted at what would happen to them in the future.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Two wordplays anticipate Esau's future. Esau sounds like the Hebrew word se‘ar, meaning "hair." Esau's later homeland was Edom. Another name for it was Seir ("hairy") because it was wooded (as though covered with hair). 

• red (Hebrew ’admoni): This Hebrew word sounds like Esau’s other name, Edom, which had red soil (Genesis 25:27–34). 

• hair like a fur coat: This suggests his unspiritual character (Genesis 25:34; Hebrews 12:16; compare Leviticus 26:22; Deuteronomy 7:22; 1 Corinthians 15:32). The description of the child uses words that emphasize the Edomites' character.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The name Jacob (Hebrew ya‘aqob, from Hebrew ‘aqeb, “heel, footprint”) was originally positive, meaning “protect” (like a rear guard), but it took on the negative meaning of “heel grabber” or “deceiver” in the context of Jacob’s deceptive, grasping, usurping character (see Genesis 27:36).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Esau became a skilled hunter, a man of the field: He was a wild man who enjoyed the wild country. 

• Jacob was a quiet man who stayed at home (literally a mature/perfect man dwelling in tents): He lived in tents and had good manners.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
Jacob and Esau developed according to their early traits (Genesis 25:24–26). 

Esau, the reddish, hairy man, cared about physical things rather than spiritual things (see Hebrews 12:16). His desires eventually overcame him and he sold his birthright. 

Jacob, the heel grabber, knew the birthright’s value. He made a ruthless deal to win it from his brother.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Each parent had a favorite child. 

• Because: Isaac loved Esau because of his hunting ability. Rebekah had a constant and unconditional love for Jacob.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Jacob was actually more cunning than Esau. The word for cooking (Hebrew wayyazed, meaning “boiling”) sounds like the word for hunter (Hebrew tsayid). While Jacob was boiling stew, he was also setting a trap for Esau, who is described as hairy and red. He may have waited a long time for this moment.

The word for cooking can also describe acting without proper limits, like water boiling over a pot. In this way, Jacob went too far when he took the promise for himself. By contrast, Abraham trusted that the promise was already his, so he was willing to give the land to others (see study note on 13:8–13). 

• Esau was tired and hungry, but his life was not in danger (Genesis 25:32; see study note on 25:33–34).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Esau focused only on his hunger. When a person is controlled by physical desires like this, there is no room for spiritual values. The text shows this clearly by using a Hebrew word (translated "Let me eat") that was often used when feeding animals.

• Edom means “red.” See study note on 25:25.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
On this occasion, Jacob proved to be the better hunter. However, strong ambition like this can be dangerous. God’s people should desire what God desires, but they must not try to gain these things by human effort (see Zechariah 4:6; Galatians 5:16–17; Ephesians 6:10–12). 

The Lord dealt strictly with Jacob to remove his sinful methods. Later, he received the promise not as Jacob the deceiver, but as Israel (which means “God fights”). God fought on his behalf (Genesis 32:28).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Esau quickly accepted what Jacob offered and fell into his trap. He ate and left so quickly that he could not have been close to death (Genesis 25:32). The final comment in the passage explains that Esau treated his birthright with contempt, as if it had no value (Hebrews 12:16). It is foolish to give up spiritual blessings just to satisfy physical desires (compare Genesis 3:6).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: This Abimelech is probably not the same person from chapter Genesis 20:20 because these events could be 90 years apart. Abimelech might have been the name of a dynasty or a title. First Samuel 21:10 mentions a later King Achish, who was also called Abimelech (Psalm 34:title).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: This section pauses Jacob’s story to focus on Isaac. Isaac’s success and wealth in chapter Genesis 26:26 show that God’s blessing had passed to him (compare Genesis 25:11), even though he sometimes failed to trust God.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
The Lord assured Isaac that the covenant promises (compare Genesis 12:2–3; Genesis 15:5–8; Genesis 17:3–8; Genesis 22:15–18; Genesis 28:13–14) would pass to him because Abraham faithfully listened to God and obeyed all his requirements, commands, decrees, and instructions. These terms were later used in Deuteronomy to describe God’s full legal covenant with Israel.

An Israelite would immediately think of the complete Torah when hearing these words and be prompted to obey God’s law as Abraham did, though Abraham had only a few commands from the Lord. Through these words, the text emphasizes that Abraham would have obeyed the later commands if he had had them, because he was an obedient servant of the Lord.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
While Isaac was living in Gerar, he, like his father Abraham, told people that his wife was his sister. Some think this story repeats the accounts of Abraham’s deception (Genesis 12:10–20; Genesis 20:1–18). But there are more differences than similarities. It is not surprising that a son repeated his father’s lie.

Genesis 26 shows, through many similar patterns, that God’s plan continued through Isaac. Even when Isaac put the covenant at risk, as Abraham had done, God prevented something terrible from happening and protected the marriage. God would bless Abraham’s descendants because of Abraham, but they still needed to trust God themselves to experience those blessings. 

True faith in God's promises leads to a life without fear as one follows him. Fear, however, can put the blessing at risk and make a person’s faith seem empty.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Abimelech … looked down … to see Isaac caressing his wife Rebekah: The Hebrew word for "caressing" is the same as the word used for Ishmael "mocking" Isaac (Genesis 21:9). This Hebrew word is also related to the name Isaac (Hebrew yitskhaq). It is as if Isaac’s lack of faith made Abimelech look foolish and brought shame on Rebekah and on the great promise connected to Isaac’s name.
