entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Isaac, like his father, was rebuked by Abimelech (see study note on 20:1–18). This legal wording would remind Israel of how important it was to preserve marital purity. Abimelech recognized the danger to his own people. Though his decree preserved his own society, it was also a word from God that preserved the sanctity of Isaac’s and Israel’s marriages. If Isaac’s marriage had ended here, there would have been no Israelite society.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Isaac lived in the land as a temporary resident. God blessed him, so his crops grew well and he became very rich.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The Philistines were jealous of Isaac's success and filled his wells with dirt. The king then told Isaac to leave the area because he was too powerful for them (compare Genesis 21:22–23).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
Isaac left … in the Valley of Gerar: This was away from the city of Gerar itself, but probably still within 16 kilometers (10 miles). 

When he got there, Isaac reopened the wells of his father. Although people opposed him there, Isaac chose not to fight back. He gave up one well after another until God's blessing overcame the opposition. Whenever Isaac reopened a well, even if enemies filled it in, he found water. God blessed Isaac, and nothing could stop it. Finally, the Philistines left Isaac alone.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Beersheba … the Lord appeared him: This was to confirm his covenant (compare Genesis 21:31–33). Isaac showed faith like his father by building an altar to the Lord. He declared the Lord’s identity and nature (see study note on 12:8; Genesis 21:33).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
This oath is like the one a previous king made with Abraham (see Genesis 21:22–31). This king acknowledged that God was blessing Isaac. He understood that an oath with Isaac would be beneficial. 

No opposition can stop God's blessing. It will flourish, and other nations will notice it. They will seek peace with God's people to share in the blessing.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Since the earlier treaty was renewed with Isaac, the name of the well was also renewed by the oath.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Esau's marriages show how he was not suitable to lead God's covenant people into receiving God's blessings. Isaac's later attempt to bless Esau was foolish (Genesis 27:1–40). Later, Esau married a third wife, trying to make things right without success (Genesis 28:6–9).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• The first scene introduces the main problem in the chapter. Isaac knew about God’s oracle (a message from God; Genesis 25:22–23), but he went against it or ignored it when he tried to bless Esau.

• Isaac was old and his eyes were so weak that he could no longer see: This shows that he was losing awareness, both physically and spiritually.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob got his father Isaac’s blessing through deception. In this story, an entire family tries to carry out their responsibilities by physical means rather than by faith. Faith would have provided Rebekah and Jacob a more honorable solution to the crisis.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Like Esau, Isaac let his love of tasty food control his affections (compare Genesis 25:28–34).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Esau agreed to Isaac’s plan. In doing so, he broke the oath he had sworn to Jacob (Genesis 25:33).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The blessing seemed to be at risk. In the second scene, Rebekah and Jacob tried to gain God’s blessing through deception, rather than through faith and love. Rebekah made a plan to trick Isaac, who was old, into thinking he was blessing Esau when he was actually blessing Jacob.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob had no problem tricking his father. He only worried it might fail and Isaac would curse him for attempting it.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob lied about his identity, and then came close to blasphemy (speaking in a way that dishonors God) by lying about God.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: In scene three, Jacob tricks his father and receives the blessing.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Isaac expressed his doubts three times. But his senses, which were not working well, eventually misled him (see study note on 27:1–4).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: In scene four, everything is discovered, and the family becomes even more divided.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: When Isaac understood what happened, he started shaking uncontrollably. He had tried to change God's plan, but God stopped him.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Esau was very bitter and angry enough to kill. After Jacob received their father’s blessing, Esau planned to take his brother’s life (Genesis 27:41).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• he has cheated me twice (or tripped me up, or deceived me): Esau started to understand Jacob's true nature. Jacob took the birthright (the right of inheritance, Hebrew bekorah; Genesis 25:27–34). He tricked their father to get the blessing (the spoken pronouncement of the inheritance, Hebrew berakah). 

• Esau was right in how he judged Jacob, but he did not recognize his own ungodliness in these actions (see study note on 27:5; Hebrews 12:16).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: There was no way to undo the blessing. Isaac had declared a message from God, who had made Jacob to be Esau’s master (see Romans 9:11–13).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: All that remained for Esau was a promise of hardship and struggle (compare Genesis 3:17–19; Genesis 16:11–12).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
Rebekah and Jacob received the blessing, but Esau hated them for it. They also separated from one another. The Bible does not indicate that Rebekah and Jacob ever saw each other again. 

They gained nothing that God would not have given them anyway. Their actions came at the expense of their relationship. Jacob had to flee from home to escape Esau's vengeance.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
Jacob met the Lord on a road that Abraham had traveled 125 years earlier. The story in Genesis 27:42–33:17 follows a pattern (called a "chiasm") focusing on Jacob’s exile: 

• A: Jacob runs away from Esau (Genesis 27:42–28:9) 

• B: Angels of God meet Jacob at Bethel (Genesis 28:10–22) 

• C: Jacob lives in exile in Paddan-aram (Genesis 29:1–31:55) 

• B’: Angels of God meet Jacob at Mahanaim (Genesis 32:1–2) 

• A’: Jacob reconciles with Esau (Genesis 32:3–33:17).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Rebekah convinced Isaac to send Jacob away by carefully planning her words and actions. Like Isaac, Jacob married a woman from his relatives who lived in the east.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Isaac stayed in the land, but Jacob had to leave. God would deal with Jacob through his uncle Laban (see study note on 29:1–31:55). 

• Believers must remain spiritually pure by marrying other believers (2 Corinthians 6:14–18). The Canaanites had many groups and clans among their people through wars, treaties, and marriages (see Genesis 34:20–23). 

Abraham’s family was to resist such mixing (compare Genesis 24:3; chapter Genesis 34:34). They were supposed to marry within their clan to maintain the purity of the line and of the faith that identified them as the chosen people. The surest way to lose their distinctiveness was to intermarry with people of other tribal backgrounds and beliefs (see Ezra 9–10; Nehemiah 13:23–29).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Before Jacob departed, Isaac gave him a pure, legitimate blessing. He did not hold back, because he now knew what God wanted him to do. Isaac clearly passed on the blessing God Almighty (Hebrew El-Shaddai; see Genesis 17:1) had given to Abraham and to him regarding prosperity and the land (compare Genesis 15:5, Genesis 15:18–20).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Esau, the unchosen son still trying to please his father, married a woman from the unchosen line of Ishmael, which he thought would be more acceptable. He did not understand the uniqueness of the covenant family.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Even though Jacob used deceptive methods to get the blessing, God promised to protect and provide for him. The God of Abraham and Isaac was also the God of Jacob. This revelation greatly changed Jacob's perspective and brought faith into clearer focus.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob set up camp in a safe spot at the base of a hill. He probably used a large stone more for protection than as a pillow.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• ladder: This word occurs nowhere else in Scripture. The image may have reminded people at that time of a stairway or ramp on the front of a ziggurat (a large temple tower in ancient Mesopotamia). Such a structure was thought to connect heaven and earth (see study note on 11:4). 

In this passage, God begins direct communication between heaven and earth to guide and protect Jacob, who carries his covenant (Genesis 28:13–15; see Psalm 91:11–15). 

• Jesus later said that he himself is the way between heaven and earth (John 1:51).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The vision showed that God and his angels were with Jacob on his journey. God reminded Jacob of the promises made to Abraham and Isaac. He promised Jacob land, descendants as numerous as dust (compare Genesis 13:16; Genesis 22:17), and blessings for all people through him (compare Genesis 12:2–3; Genesis 15:5, Genesis 15:18; Genesis 17:3–8; Genesis 22:15–18; Genesis 35:11–12). God also promised to be with Jacob and protect him until he returned.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob inherited Abraham’s entire covenant (see Genesis 22:17), which confirmed Isaac’s blessing (Genesis 28:3–4) and showed that Jacob would live away from home for a time (Genesis 28:15; see Genesis 15:12–16).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: I am with you: The promise of God’s presence meant that God would protect and provide for Jacob in a special way. God’s promise to be with his people is repeated throughout Scripture (see also Genesis 26:24). It encourages those who have faith to respond with worship and confidence (Genesis 28:16–22).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
The second part of the passage describes Jacob's response to God's revelation. He felt reverence and awe in God's presence. His acts of devotion became models for Israel's worship. 

When God graciously visits his people and promises to be with them and make them a blessing to the world, his people respond in faith with reverence, worship, offerings, and vows. They preserve their faith in memory for future worshipers.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Anointing with oil became a way of setting something apart for divine use in Israel’s worship (Exodus 29:1–7; Exodus 40:9; Leviticus 2:1; 1 Samuel 10:1).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Bethel later became a holy site for Israel (see Judges 20:18–27; 1 Samuel 7:16; 1 Samuel 10:3; 1 Kings 12:26–13:10; 2 Kings 2:2–3).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: In view of what God would do for him, Jacob vowed to do certain things for God. He believed the Lord’s words and responded in gratitude. Jacob’s vow influenced Israel’s way of making commitments to God in worship.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: I will surely You a tenth: By paying a tithe (a tenth) as an act of worship, a person acknowledges that everything is a gift from God and belongs to God (see Genesis 14:19–20; Numbers 18:21–32; Deuteronomy 14:22–29; 2 Chronicles 31:5–6; Malachi 3:7–12; Matthew 23:23).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
Jacob resumed his journey: The Hebrew text can be literally translated as he "lifted up his feet," suggesting he felt inspired. He continued his journey with renewed enthusiasm. This change in attitude came from the vision he received at Bethel. 

It was a wonderful revelation that God would protect and bless him. Now, he expected God's promises to come true, not only to escape from Esau. Jacob’s attitude had become positive and magnanimous to the point of being naive and vulnerable.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• These chapters describe how God fulfilled his promise by greatly blessing Jacob with a family and possessions. God also disciplined Jacob, leaving him to struggle with Laban for many years. Laban was Jacob’s match in deception, and thus a means of correction. 

• The story of Jacob and Laban is similar to Israel's later stay in Egypt. Jacob struggled while serving his uncle but finally emerged with a large family (the founders of the 12 tribes) and great wealth. In Egypt, the Israelites suffered under their oppressors, but they also flourished, becoming a great nation of 12 large tribes and escaping with great riches.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob met Rachel at the well at just the right time. This happened under God’s guidance, because God rules over all things (God is sovereign). God was leading Jacob toward the fulfillment of his promises (see Genesis 24:12–20). The well was a reminder of God’s blessing (compare Genesis 16:13–14; Genesis 21:19; Genesis 26:19–25, Genesis 26:33).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Unlike the lazy, unhelpful shepherds (Genesis 29:7–8), this verse shows Jacob to be generous, hardworking, and energetic. 

• watered his uncle's sheep: Laban's flocks would thrive under Jacob's care.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob kissed Rachel: Kissing relatives was an appropriate way to greet them (Genesis 29:13; compare Song 8:1).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: You are indeed my own flesh and blood: Laban welcomed Jacob into his house and treated him much like a son.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
Jacob looked forward with joy to marrying Rachel, but this hope became a time of testing. Laban acted with shrewdness (clever but not honest behavior), and Jacob was disciplined (corrected and trained). Jacob and his mother had deceived his father and brother to gain the blessing. Now Laban, his mother’s brother, deceived him.

Jacob experienced the results of his own dishonesty through 20 years of hard work, suffering, and being misled while serving Laban (Genesis 31:38). 

In God’s fair judgment, people receive what they do (Galatians 6:7). Laban’s actions helped Jacob see his own tendency to deceive others. God often brings people into the lives of believers to discipline them. But Jacob was determined, and God greatly blessed him with a large family and many possessions during this time of service (Genesis 30:25–43).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Seven years of service was a high bride-price in the ancient world, but Rachel was beautiful (like Sarah and Rebekah), and Jacob was in love with her.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Like Isaac, Jacob was given food and wine (compare Genesis 27:25). He could not see in the darkness (compare Genesis 27:1). He became confused by clothing (compare Genesis 27:15) and misled by touch (compare Genesis 27:23). 

• The marriage had already been completed (the husband and wife had come together as one; Genesis 29:23; compare Genesis 2:24). Because of this, Jacob was bound to Leah.

• It is not our custom here to give the younger daughter in marriage before the older: Laban's words are a reminder of what Jacob did when he, the younger son, pretended to be his older brother to gain the blessing (chapter Genesis 27:27). Now Leah, the older sister, pretended to be the younger sister to get a husband. God gave the deceiver a dose of his own deception as a discipline in his life.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: After the bridal week ended, Jacob also married Rachel (Genesis 29:27). But he had to work another seven years (see Genesis 31:41). Laban seemed to have the advantage.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: he loved Rachel more than Leah: This kind of favoritism (showing special love to one person over others) caused ongoing trouble in his family (see Genesis 25:28; Genesis 37:3). Jacob’s favoritism had lasting effects. His family was often divided, and their descendants (the tribes of Israel) were rarely united.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Leah’s first four sons were born in rapid succession, but Rachel could not conceive. She was unable to have children, like Sarah and Rebekah (compare Genesis 16:1; Genesis 25:21; see also 1 Samuel 1:1–28; Luke 1:5–25).

• Each name is a memorable wordplay on Leah’s experience and hopes.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• The rivalry between these sisters explains much of the later conflict among their sons, and then among the tribes. This is similar to how Jacob and Laban's rivalry predicted future conflicts between Israel and the Arameans of Damascus (2 Samuel 8:5–6; 2 Samuel 10:8–19; 1 Kings 20:1–34; 2 Kings 5:1–8:29; 2 Kings 13:1–25; Isaiah 7:1–9). 

• God fights for the cause of the poor and oppressed. He honored Leah, the despised first wife, by making her the first mother. Judah's royal tribe and Levi's priestly line came from her. This was despite Jacob's favoritism for Rachel and her children. 

Despite the tension and jealousy resulting from Laban’s deceit and Jacob’s favoritism, God still grew Jacob’s family and brought about the births of the tribal ancestors.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
The LORD has seen my affliction: The name Reuben (from the Hebrew re’uben) sounds like the Hebrew phrase ra‘ah be‘onyi, which means “he has seen my affliction.” Leah felt that God had seen her suffering and had comforted her when her son was born, and she hoped that Jacob would now love her. 

Jacob did not notice her suffering, but God did (compare Genesis 16:14; Genesis 24:62; Genesis 25:11). The name was a reminder of God’s care and help.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Leah named her second son Simeon. The name suggests that she had cried out to the Lord and was heard (compare Genesis 16:11).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Leah named her third son Levi because she hoped her husband would become attached to her after she had borne him three sons. The name Levi sounds like the Hebrew word for “attached” or “joined.” But this did not happen.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Leah accepted that Jacob would never love her. She named her fourth son Judah, saying, "I will praise the Lord." In Hebrew, Judah means "praised." She appeared to have stopped hoping for Jacob's love and found comfort in the Lord.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: In that culture, for a woman not to have children could feel like a kind of death (compare 1 Samuel 1:1 Samuel 1). Only God could enable Rachel to have children.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Rachel’s naming of sons through Bilhah does not reflect faith as Leah’s namings had. Rachel felt wronged over the marriage and her barrenness. The names of Bilhah’s sons reflect Rachel’s bitter struggle with her sister and her feeling of some victory.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Rachel decided to have children through her servant, and Jacob agreed. This is similar to Sarai using Hagar (Genesis 16:1–4).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Dan means “he judged” or “he vindicated.” Rachel felt justified (Hebrew dananni) by Dan’s birth.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The name Naphtali is related to the phrase In my great struggles. In Hebrew, the phrase is naptule ’elohim niptalti, which means “I have struggled the struggles of God.”

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: When Leah saw that she had stopped having children, she gave her servant Zilpah to Jacob as a wife, even though she already had four sons.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Gad (meaning "fortune") was the name of a god associated with fortune. Asher (meaning "happy") was the name of a god associated with luck. These names show Leah's pagan background, but there is no indication she believed in these gods.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: People believed mandrakes could increase sexual desire and help women become pregnant (see Song 7:13). Rachel hoped they would help her become pregnant, so she made a deal with Leah. Rachel would let Leah spend one night with Jacob in exchange for mandrakes. Yet, Leah became pregnant, not Rachel.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The name Issachar reflects this idea of being hired or receiving payment. It reminds readers of the events surrounding his birth. Leah says that Jacob was "hired” for the night (Genesis 30:16). The Hebrew word sekari means “my hire.”

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Zebulun means "honor" or "gift," like a dowry or tribute. Leah believed God gave her Zebulun so her husband would honor her. She always hoped this would happen.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Dinah was the only daughter of Jacob. See chapter Genesis 34:34.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Rachel finally had her own son, Joseph, thanks to God's intervention. His birth was not due to superstitions (Genesis 30:14–16) or the custom of giving servants as wives. 

• The Hebrew word translated as "taken away" (’asap) sounds similar to the name Joseph (yosep), which means "may he add." Rachel was happy about Joseph's birth and prayed for another son.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: After working for fourteen years, Jacob asked Laban if he could return home. The two nomadic leaders negotiated politely but stayed cautious. Laban wanted more from Jacob, while Jacob wanted to earn his wages through selective breeding.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: blessed me: God made Laban successful because Jacob was with him (see Genesis 22:18). Laban may have looked for signs (omens) to understand what was happening, or he may simply have noticed the results. Dark-colored sheep were uncommon (Genesis 30:32). So, people considered having many of this color as a sign of God's blessing.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob agreed that God had blessed Laban through him, so he made a plan to gain something for himself. He proposed for his wages the rare black and multicolored goats and the speckled and spotted sheep that were born.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: As Abraham had done with Lot (Genesis 13:9), Jacob gave Laban what he valued most. White sheep were more common and more valuable than dark or multicolored sheep; as a man of faith, Jacob was willing to take the rejects (compare 1 Corinthians 1:26).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Laban said he agreed with Jacob’s plan, but he tried to prevent Jacob from gaining wealth by removing animals from the flock that would fulfill the agreement. 

• Laban's deception with the goats is similar to Jacob's deception with Esau (compare Genesis 27:9; see study note on 29:14–30).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: exposing the white inner wood: This clever wordplay explains the entire section. When Jacob exposed the white (Hebrew laban) streaks of wood underneath, he played the "white" game (the Laban game) and won. By outsmarting Laban ("Whitey"), Jacob's flocks increased and he became successful.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
God blessed Jacob even though Laban was deceitful. Jacob cleverly used selective breeding to grow his flock. He followed the traditional belief that peeled sticks could affect the type of animals born. 

The peeled branches seemed to help his animals produce streaked and spotted offspring. Jacob later admitted that God had helped him succeed (Genesis 31:7–12). Jacob ended up with stronger animals, while Laban got the weaker ones (Genesis 30:41–42).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Laban now received what he deserved for how he treated Jacob. His attempt to cheat Jacob led to Jacob gaining more, because God was working in Jacob’s life.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob became very wealthy, in fulfillment of God’s promises to him (Genesis 27:28; Genesis 28:13–15).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Laban’s sons became more hostile toward Jacob because his flocks were growing faster than theirs. They were jealous because God was blessing Jacob. They were also afraid that he might take over everything they had.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob’s return journey led to a conflict with Laban. This conflict created a lasting boundary between Israel (Jacob) and Aram (Laban). God kept his promise to Jacob. He made Jacob successful in Paddan-aram and protected him as he traveled back home.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• the land of your fathers was Canaan, to which God had called Abraham (Genesis 12:1–7; Genesis 17:8). 

• Go back … I will be with you: See study notes on 26:2–5; 28:12–15. God protected Jacob (also called “Israel,” Genesis 32:28) as he led his family back to the land God promised them. Later, God brought Israel back to Canaan after many years of slavery in Egypt. 

This return had many similarities to this passage:

• God defeated foreign gods and beliefs. 

• He used dreams for rescue and protection. 

• He gave victory over threats. 

• He set boundaries between nations and tribes (see Deuteronomy 32:8).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob explained to his wives how God had blessed him, even though Laban opposed him. He was not sure if they wanted to leave Laban and move to Canaan. He wanted his family to agree willingly, so he needed to persuade them. He shared how God had guided and provided for them over the years. He explained that he needed to keep the vow he made at Bethel (Genesis 28:20–22).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The women quickly agreed to go with Jacob because God had blessed him. They were very willing to leave Laban, who had wasted their wealth (the property meant to support them). They understood that what God gave Jacob would also belong to them.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob left Laban secretly because he was afraid of revenge (Genesis 31:31).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Rachel stole her father’s household idols: She might have wanted to recover some of the wealth Laban wasted. She may have also worshiped idols (compare Genesis 35:2–4). Having the idols might have meant claiming the family inheritance, as later customs indicate. Laban seemed to feel insecure without them. Whatever her reasons, Rachel's theft nearly caused disaster for the family when Laban overtook them. 

• A wordplay shows that Rachel and Jacob were very similar—Rachel stole (Hebrew wattignob) Laban's household gods. Jacob tricked (Hebrew wayyignob, "stole the heart of, deceived") Laban.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The journey took the family from Haran southwest to the land of Gilead, just east of the Jordan River in the north of today’s kingdom of Jordan.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• The theft of the idols (Genesis 31:19) probably caused Laban and his men to chase Jacob. It was one thing for Jacob to take his family and flocks (Laban probably still thought they were his). But taking the household gods was different. Laban might have feared Jacob would return to claim all of Laban’s property. When he could not find the gods, he asked for a treaty to keep Jacob away (Genesis 31:43–53). 

• It took Laban seven days to overtake Jacob.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Be careful not to say anything to Jacob, either good or bad: God told Laban not to try to bring justice himself. When we try to enact our own sense of good and evil apart from God’s command, we always do evil (see study note on 2:9).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The dispute between the two men used the language of legal controversies and lawsuits (see also Genesis 31:36). Laban first argued that Jacob had wronged him by stealing from him.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob was so sure he did not have the gods that he made an oath that unknowingly put Rachel under a death sentence.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Laban searched for the idols but did not find them. He did not think that a woman in her monthly bleeding would make the idols ceremonially unclean by sitting on them (see Leviticus 15:19–24).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob answered by accusing Laban of making false charges and humiliating him. Now Laban was the one who had to answer, because his charges were insulting and seemed to have no basis.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob, who preferred life at home (Genesis 25:27), had spent 20 years enduring the hardships of outdoor life, which Esau had loved.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
the Fear of Isaac: This is a name for God used here and in Genesis 31:53. It does not mean that Isaac was afraid of God in a negative way. Here, fear means deep respect, honor, and awe for God.

God was with Jacob (Genesis 31:3). God saw Jacob’s hard work and faithfulness, even though Laban treated him badly. God rewarded Jacob. Laban’s dream showed Jacob that he was right.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Laban wanted a treaty to end the dispute because he felt unsafe and wanted to secure the borders. Jacob did not need a treaty because God had provided for him and protected him.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The stone and the pillar marked the border agreement between the two men. It was a witness for future generations. Each man named the monument witness in his own language. It became the lasting border between Israel and the kingdom of Aram (Syria), two nations often at war.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The pile of stones was also called Mizpah (which means “watchtower”). God would watch over Jacob and Laban to keep them apart, because they did not trust each other.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Laban added conditions to the treaty to try to justify himself. He used many words to hide his own dishonesty and make Jacob look unethical. He even claimed credit for the monument Jacob had built ("here is the pillar I have set up," Genesis 31:51). The women and children would be safer and better cared for with Jacob than they ever were with Laban.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: God promised Jacob protection when he needed comfort the most. Jacob's journey was a physical return to his homeland and a spiritual return to God's promised land. God protects his people and fulfills his plan.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• This is the camp of God: Jacob probably saw the angels as a sign of God's protection, similar to the earlier vision when he left the land (Genesis 28:10–22). 

• Mahanaim (meaning “two camps”): Jacob's group and the group of angels were together in one place.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Apparently inspired by the vision of angels (Genesis 32:1, Hebrew mal’akim), Jacob sent messengers (mal’akim) into Edom to meet Esau.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob divided his company into two groups or camps (Hebrew makhanoth, related to "Mahanaim" in Genesis 32:2). This was because he was afraid. Jacob remembered Esau's character and his threat to kill him (see Genesis 25:25; Genesis 27:41).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob’s prayer is a wonderful example of how to address God. He based his appeal on God’s will, reminding God of his relationship with him, his command for him to return to the land, and his promise (Genesis 32:9). He had a correct attitude of genuine humility and total dependence on God (Genesis 32:10). Finally, he asked that God rescue him from his brother, and he repeated God’s promises (see Genesis 22:17).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Taking a large portion of the wealth God had blessed him with (some 550 animals), Jacob prepared a gift to appease Esau’s anger and gain his favor.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
The Jabbok River flows westward to the Jordan Valley, dividing the region of Bashan on the north from Gilead on the south. 

Wordplays on Jacob’s name and character preserve the memory of this encounter. Jacob (Hebrew ya‘aqob), while at Jabbok (Hebrew yabboq), wrestled (Hebrew wayye’abeq). Through his fight with an adversary to receive the blessing, Jacob’s name would be changed, and his deceptive striving would partially give way to faith as his way of life.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob went back to the land God promised him. Before this, God met, injured, and blessed him. God also changed his name to Israel. This event was a significant turning point for Jacob.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• a man wrestled: The story develops just as it did for Jacob. We do not know any details about the attacker, who later refused to reveal his identity (Genesis 32:29). 

• until daybreak: The darkness matched Jacob’s situation, adding to his fear and uncertainty. In the dark, he could not tell who it was. It might have been one of Esau’s or Laban’s men.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: he struck the socket of Jacob’s hip and dislocated it: Jacob, who had struggled and deceived others, could no longer fight. When the man wrestled with him as an equal, Jacob could hold his ground. But now he met someone far stronger than himself.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: At daybreak, Jacob began to understand the meaning of the struggle. He realized who his opponent was. Since he could not win by fighting, he held on and asked for God’s blessing.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: What is your name?: The Lord's question was about Jacob's character, not just his identity (see Genesis 3:9; Genesis 4:9). By stating his name, Jacob admitted his nature and behavior as a "Heel-grabber, Deceiver, Usurper." Before God would bless him, Jacob needed to recognize who he was. Then God would change his identity.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Jacob: See study note on 25:26. 

• Israel (“God fights”): God first fought with him, but now God would fight for him. Jacob’s name promised hope for him and his descendants. 

• you have struggled with God and with men: Throughout his life, Jacob tried to get God’s blessing using his own skills and by any means necessary. He understood the importance of the blessing but was too self-reliant and proud to accept it freely. He had been fighting God long before this encounter. 

• and have prevailed: He had succeeded in his struggles with Esau and with Laban. Now he received God’s blessing.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob knew who was with him (Genesis 32:30). The request was his attempt to regain some control. God would not reveal his name, which cannot be had on demand.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Peniel (which means “face of God”): The name shows that Jacob recognized the man as a manifestation of God (a theophany). 

• yet my life was spared (or and my soul has been rescued): This probably meant Jacob realized that God had answered his prayer to be saved from Esau (Genesis 32:11). If he could encounter God like this and survive, he had nothing to fear from Esau. The saying may also reflect an ancient belief that no one can see God and live (see Exodus 33:20).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
God injured Jacob’s hip. This limited Jacob’s pride and self-reliance (depending on his own strength). Because God reduced his natural strength, Jacob had to trust the Lord more.

Jacob thought he could return to his land by outsmarting his brother again (Genesis 32:3–21). But at the border of the land, he met its true owner. He would receive the land, but only if God fought for him.

Self-reliance (trying to gain God’s blessing by our own strength or by worldly ways) will not succeed. If we continue in this way, God may need to weaken our self-reliance so that we trust him more.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The story includes a dietary restriction for Israel that became a custom but was not put into law. This custom helped preserve the memory of the story. Observant Jews still refuse to eat the tendons of an animal’s hindquarters.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
God had changed Jacob's identity (Genesis 32:27–28), but he had not yet learned to live in line with his new name. He still showed favoritism (treating some family members better than others), which can divide families. 

He arranged his family and possessions according to their importance to him. He placed the servant wives and their children in front, where they would face danger first. Leah and her children were behind them. Rachel and Joseph were at the back, where it was safest.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
Jacob had long expected to meet his brother Esau, and the meeting turned out much better than he feared. Esau’s changed heart shows how “God fights” for his people (See Genesis 32:28). God works powerfully for his people when they trust him.

Earlier, Esau did not value his birthright (the rights and blessing of the firstborn son; Genesis 25:32–34). Now he no longer held on to old anger. Jacob understood that God had stepped in and changed the situation.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
Jacob was scared even though he had no reason to be. He tried to calm his brother by acting like a servant to a king:

• he bowed (Genesis 33:3), 

• used respectful titles (Genesis 33:8, Genesis 33:13), 

• introduced people (Genesis 33:6–7), and 

• gave gifts (Genesis 33:8).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Esau’s friendly greeting was an answer to prayer (Genesis 32:11). God had rescued Jacob from Esau’s revenge.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: your servant: When speaking with his brother, Jacob kept calling himself Esau’s servant (also Genesis 33:14). He referred to Esau as his lord (Genesis 33:8, Genesis 33:13–15). Esau called Jacob “my brother” (Genesis 33:9). Jacob acted carefully to avoid any possible attack from Esau. In doing this, he went against the earlier oracle (a message from God about the future; Genesis 25:23).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Among Jacob’s sons, only Joseph is named. Joseph was Jacob’s favorite son and the recipient of the blessing.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob knew that Esau’s friendly greeting was God’s work, secured at Peniel when he saw God face to face.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: my gift (literally my blessing) that was brought to you: Jacob considered Esau as a threat and tried to calm him with a gift (see 2 Kings 17:3–4; 2 Kings 18:7, 2 Kings 18:14; 2 Chronicles 28:21). He might have felt guilty and wanted to fix past mistakes. Jacob insisted that Esau accept the gift.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Even though Esau seemed generous, Jacob was cautious and cleverly avoided traveling with him. 

• until I come to my lord at Seir: Jacob's lie shows his old habit of using deceit instead of living by faith.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob promised Esau he would follow him south to Seir, but he deceived him. Instead, Jacob went to Succoth, which is east of the Jordan River and north of the Jabbok.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• These verses conclude Jacob's adventures away from home. He returned safely with a large family and many possessions. 

• Jacob, like Abraham, built an altar at Shechem (see Genesis 12:6–8) and bought land from Hamor's family.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: El-Elohe-Israel: The name of the altar means "God, the God of Israel." It commemorated Jacob's relationship with God. Jacob publicly declared that God was his God and had guided him back to the land he would inherit.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Dinah was probably Jacob's only daughter (Genesis 30:21). 

• Shechem … saw her, he took her and lay with her by force: Shechem took Dinah and raped her, which ruined her chances for a proper marriage.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
After Jacob and his family settled in the land, the Canaanites became a threat. This story warns the Israelites about the risk of being influenced by the Canaanites. Later, God commanded Israel not to marry or make deals with them because they were corrupt and would corrupt others. This chapter gives an implicit warning against adopting their lifestyle (Genesis 34:1–2). 

It also teaches Israel to maintain integrity and not misuse holy things for deceit or violence (Genesis 34:13). Israel's reputation was at risk in the land (Genesis 34:30). Because of their violent actions, Simeon and Levi did not receive the birthright blessing (Genesis 49:5–7).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
Shechem had strong feelings for Dinah, and he was willing to go through great trouble because of her (Genesis 34:11–12, Genesis 34:17–18, Genesis 34:24). However, the way he showed his “love” (not true love, but a selfish desire) was impulsive and self-centered. It also broke accepted moral standards of that time (compare Judges 14:2; see 1 Corinthians 13:4–7; 1 John 4:10). 

His character shows why Israel needed to stay separate from the Canaanites (the people living in the land at that time).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
Jacob’s response to this crime is surprising. When he heard that Dinah had been defiled, he said nothing about it until his sons came home. Because Jacob did not act, his sons did, though without the wisdom and integrity necessary for justice. 

Dinah’s full brothers were shocked and furious that Shechem had done such a disgraceful thing to Jacob’s family (literally in Israel; this is the first use of the name Israel to describe the family). This sexual crime was an outrage against the community of God’s people and deserved punishment, but the leader of the clan did nothing.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
Hamor suggested a marriage alliance for mutual economic gain. But God had already promised Jacob everything, including the land (Genesis 34:10; see Genesis 14:21–24). Hamor wanted to control Israel’s wealth (Genesis 34:23). Trusting the Canaanites would not lead to anything good.

For some of these reasons, the law of Moses did not allow Israelites to marry Canaanites (see Exodus 23:27–33; Deuteronomy 7:1–5). The exception would be if they converted (see Joshua 2:1–15; Joshua 6:23–25; Matthew 1:5).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Dinah’s brothers responded to the proposal without waiting for Jacob to respond, and they acted deceitfully. They may not have thought that Shechem and his people would ever agree to the rite of circumcision, but they knew what they would do if the Canaanites accepted (Genesis 34:25).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The Canaanite men agreed to the condition, and every male in the town was circumcised. This was not only to allow Shechem to marry Dinah. They also saw it as a way to gain everything that Jacob owned (Genesis 34:23).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
When Simeon and Levi used circumcision (the sign of God’s covenant) to deceive and kill the Canaanite men, they showed disrespect for that sacred sign. Their killing of all the males and their looting of the city was not justice. It was harsh and excessive revenge.

They were angry and wanted to correct a wrong. But they should have asked for payment for the harm done (see Exodus 22:16–17; Deuteronomy 22:28–29). Instead, their violent anger led to the loss of their birthright blessing (the special family blessing given to the firstborn; Genesis 49:5–7).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob responded again fearfully because of what might happen to him. But God made the people of the land fear him instead (Genesis 35:5).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob returned to Bethel, about 24 kilometers (15 miles) south of Shechem, to fulfill the vows he made there (Genesis 28:20–22).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• This chapter discusses God's promises, Jacob's vow, and how Jacob's sons continue the covenant. Deborah, Rachel, and Isaac died. This marked the end of an era and the story of Isaac's family (Genesis 25:19–35:29). 

• They removed idols (Genesis 35:1–4) and established pure worship (Genesis 35:6–7). During this time, they needed to renew their faith so Jacob's sons could continue the covenant.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob vowed to fully devote himself to the Lord (Genesis 28:20–22). To establish this devotion, his family had to get rid of all pagan idols and stop worshiping other gods. God allows no rivals. Only the Lord could be their God (compare Joshua 5:1–9).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: He has been with me wherever I have gone: God had fulfilled his promises (Genesis 28:15; Genesis 31:3), so Jacob must fulfill his vow.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: a terror from God: People had heard about the killing of the men of Shechem (Genesis 34:25–30).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob built an altar at Bethel as God had instructed (Genesis 35:1; compare Genesis 12:8).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: At Bethel, God confirmed the promise he made earlier. He reminded Jacob that his name was now Israel, proving that he had received the blessing.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: God’s reference to himself as God Almighty assured Jacob that his promise could and would be fulfilled. At Bethel, God promised Jacob that he would have descendants in the land (compare Genesis 28:13–14). Here, God added that his descendants would include kings (see Genesis 17:6).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: In fulfilling his vow (Genesis 28:20–22), Jacob’s actions were almost identical to his actions in the earlier experience at Bethel (compare Genesis 28:16–19).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Benjamin's birth completed the family. But it was a sad event because Rachel died during childbirth (see study note on 31:32).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Rachel felt that the name Ben-oni, meaning “son of my sorrow,” fit the moment. But Jacob did not want his son to carry such a sad name, so he changed it to Benjamin, meaning “son of my right hand.” In this way, Jacob changed a moment of sorrow into one of hope and gave his son a name that pointed to blessing and strength.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob did not carry Rachel’s body to the family tomb at Machpelah (Genesis 23:1–20; Genesis 25:9; Genesis 49:30; Genesis 50:13) but buried her in the territory that would be Benjamin’s (see Josh 18:21–28; 1 Sam 10:2).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: it marks Rachel’s tomb to this day: This seems to be a later editorial comment by someone who was living in the land after the conquest and giving directions to the tomb (see Genesis Book Introduction, “Composition”).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Reuben had sexual relations with Bilhah. This dishonored his father's marriage. As the oldest son, Reuben might have been trying to take over as the clan leader using a pagan method (compare 2 Samuel 16:15–22). But this act caused him to lose his birthright (see Genesis 49:3–4). 

• Jacob soon found out what happened, but he delayed his response again (see Genesis 49:3–4; compare Genesis 34:5).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The 12 sons of Jacob became the leaders of the 12 tribes of Israel. Their names are the beginnings of the nation.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Esau and Jacob, listed in the order of their birth, reunited to bury Isaac in Hebron. This was probably their first meeting since they reconciled (see Genesis 33:16–17; Genesis 13:18; Genesis 23:1–2, Genesis 23:17–19).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
The story of Esau emphasizes two main points: 

• The sons of Esau … were born to him in the land of Canaan (Genesis 36:5) before he moved to Seir (Genesis 36:8). In contrast, most of Jacob’s children were born outside Canaan but later moved there. God gave the land to Jacob and his descendants, making space for them by settling Esau elsewhere. 

• Esau was also known as Edom. Israel often had conflicts with the Edomites (see 1 Samuel 21:7; 1 Samuel 22:9–22; Obadiah 1).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Genesis now turns to the story of Isaac’s sons. It first finishes the account of Esau’s line (chapter Genesis 36:36), who was not chosen. Then it continues with the line of Jacob (chapter Genesis 37:37), whom God chose.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Oholibamah was the great-granddaughter of Seir the Horite. Seir's descendants lived in Edom when Esau went to live there (Genesis 36:20, Genesis 36:25).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Esau had three wives named Adah, Oholibamah, and Basemath. Two of these names differ from earlier mentions (Genesis 26:34; Genesis 28:9). It is possible the other wives died, Esau preferred these three out of six, or these were different names for the same wives. There is not enough information to know for sure.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Esau, like Lot, left for the eastern land (compare Genesis 13:5–6).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: This passage names the descendants of Esau's five sons.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: This passage begins a second account of Esau’s descendants (Genesis 36:1). It introduces a new list of his family line and traces his descendants through later generations. It also records marriages and alliances

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Thirteen of Esau’s descendants held leadership positions over different clans. This begins to show Esau as an overlord (a ruler over other rulers) of tribes (compare Genesis 36:40–43).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Seir the Horite was among the early people of the land. His descendants lived in that region until Esau and his descendants moved in and drove them out (Deuteronomy 2:12).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: before any king reigned over the Israelites: This editorial note was probably inserted into the text after Israel was ruled by kings (see study note on 35:20).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: It is not clear how these kings of Edom were related to Esau. The clans in Edom followed the same pattern of organization as the later tribes of Israel. They eventually chose a king from one of their tribes and carried on a line of succession from him.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
These leaders came from Esau, a great and powerful ruler. As the ancestor of the Edomites, he governed clans and regions. Eleven chiefs descended from him. 

By separating from Jacob, Esau started to free himself from Jacob's control (Genesis 27:39–40).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
In chapter Genesis 36:36, Esau was increasing in power and wealth. In contrast, Jacob, still waiting for the promise, lived in the land as a foreigner, like his father. He remained a temporary resident with a single family. 

Worldly greatness often comes more quickly than spiritual greatness. Waiting for the promised spiritual blessing while others prosper tests patience, faith, and perseverance.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• The account of Jacob and his family now turns to Joseph and his brothers. Jacob is still important, but the story focuses on Joseph, who is introduced as an obedient seventeen-year-old son.

• he brought their father a bad report about them: Bringing a bad report is not popular, but it was the right thing to do. It shows that Joseph was faithful from the beginning. As the story continues, his brothers’ wicked behavior becomes clearer. In the end, like Cain, they even tried to kill the brother who pleased God.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• The story of Joseph and his brothers is a distinct section in Genesis. It has a different tone and focus from the earlier parts. The story follows one connected series of events, with Joseph at the center.

• Repeated themes structure the entire story of Joseph. These themes are similar to those in wisdom books like Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and Daniel. 

Similar events that happen more than once shape the whole story. Its themes are like those in wisdom books (books that teach how to live well), such as Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and Daniel. These books teach that God can bring good out of evil and joy out of suffering. 

Even if this does not fully happen in this life, it will happen in the life to come. Although the wicked may succeed for a time, the righteous (those who live rightly before God) should remain faithful. A deeper and lasting way of life comes through obedience to God.

Anyone who hopes to be a leader in God’s plan can learn from Joseph’s story. Wisdom guided him and led to his success. Jesus Christ perfectly lived out this wisdom because he is the wisdom of God.

• Judah is also an important person in the story. At first, he was careless and unkind, like his brothers. But later, he truly repented (turned away from his sin). He was willing to give his life to save a younger brother for his father. Because of this, he received an important inheritance.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Israel (or Jacob): See also Genesis 37:13. 

• Israel loved Joseph more than his other children. Joseph was born when Israel was old. He was the first son of Israel's favorite wife, Rachel. 

• Israel gave Joseph a beautiful robe to show he planned to give him the largest share of the inheritance.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob’s favoritism (treating one child better than the others) toward Joseph made his other sons hate him even more. In the same way, Isaac’s and Rebekah’s favoritism had divided their family. Now Jacob’s favoritism would lead to separation between him and his son Joseph.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: God confirmed his choice of this faithful son as the future leader of the family through two symbolic dreams. This is the first of three dream sequences in chapters Genesis 37:37–50 (see Genesis 40:1–41:36; compare Genesis 15:13; Genesis 20:3; Genesis 28:12–15; Genesis 31:24). Dreams were often seen as a way God spoke to people. People considered a dream to be more important if it was given twice (repeated to show it was certain).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The sheaves of grain suggest how Joseph would gain authority over his family (see Genesis 42:1–3).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
The brothers reacted angrily to the revelation, unlike Joseph, who was honest and faithful. This shows why they were not chosen as leaders. Leaders in God's plan cannot be full of jealousy and hatred. 

In their anger, they missed an important part of the revelation. They also would become rulers ("stars," Genesis 37:9) and would successfully gather their sheaves (Genesis 37:7).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: the sun and moon and eleven stars: Signs like the sun, moon, and stars often stand for rulers. The dream showed that Joseph would become a leader over the whole family of Israel.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: your mother … and I: Joseph's birth mother, Rachel, was dead (Genesis 35:19). Leah was now the matriarch of the clan.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Joseph’s brothers hated him because they were jealous. Instead of recognizing that God was at work, they tried to stop his dreams from coming true (Genesis 37:18–36). These actions show that they were not ready to lead God’s people.

God’s choice of a leader (especially someone young or who seems unqualified) often reveals what is in people’s hearts. It shows whether they are willing to accept that leader’s authority. Joseph’s brothers represent many people throughout history who act with envy (jealous anger) and malice (a desire to harm others) because they are not committed to doing the Lord’s will.

• Jacob wondered what the dreams meant because he knew God would choose the next leader. He understood that God could choose the younger son to lead the older ones and could reveal all this in dreams.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: It was foolish for Jacob to send Joseph on such a mission, knowing how the brothers felt about him. Joseph obeyed his father by going to find his brothers despite their hatred for him.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The brothers traveled over a wide area. Shechem was about 80 kilometers (about 50 miles) from Hebron. Dothan was another 24 kilometers (15 miles) beyond Shechem.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: When Joseph's brothers saw him coming, they plotted to kill … that dreamer and stop his dreams. Earlier, they had unjustly killed the men of Shechem to avenge their sister (chapter Genesis 34:34). Now, in the region of Shechem, they plotted to unjustly kill their own brother out of jealousy.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Reuben might have been trying to regain his father's favor (Genesis 35:22) by acting as the firstborn leader (compare Genesis 42:22). Reuben succeeded in saving Joseph's life, but he did not win his father's favor (Genesis 37:29–30).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The repeated theme of changed clothes points to changes in status, position, and authority (see Genesis 37:3, Genesis 37:23; Genesis 38:14, Genesis 38:19; Genesis 39:15–18; Genesis 41:14, Genesis 41:42).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The Ishmaelite traders were descendants of the slave child who was cast out for mocking Isaac. Now they would enslave Joseph. When he was sold for 20 pieces of silver and carried to Egypt, he was at least preserved alive.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Judah began to take a leadership role, which he continued to develop as the story goes on (see Genesis 43:8–10).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• The Ishmaelites are called Midianite traders (that is, traders from Midian). Ishmaelites were descendants of Abraham through Hagar (Genesis 16:5). Midianites were descendants of Abraham through Keturah (Genesis 25:1–2). The term Ishmaelite may have been used more generally for desert tribes (nomadic groups who move from place to place). The Midianites may also have been traveling with a separate group of Ishmaelite traders (Genesis 37:27). 

• Kidnapping (taking a person by force) is mentioned in Genesis 40:15. Later, it became a capital offense (a crime punished by death) in Israel’s law (see Exodus 21:16).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: When Reuben returned, he tore his clothes in grief. His attempt to restore his relationship with his father by saving Joseph had gone wrong.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The family’s long pattern of deception influenced the brothers. Jacob had used a young goat to deceive Isaac (Genesis 27:5–17). Now Jacob’s sons deceived him using a goat (see study note on 30:34–36).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: your son's: The brothers were so full of hatred that they did not call Joseph by name or acknowledge him as their brother (see Genesis 21:10).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: recognized: Compare with Genesis 27:23.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob tore his clothes, put sackcloth around his waist: This showed his extreme distress and mourning (see Genesis 44:13; Job 1:20; Job 16:15). Jacob was devastated and refused to be comforted. This betrayal affected his entire family.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: sold Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar: Joseph worked in a position that matched his potential for leadership, but he still faced more testing.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
The story of Judah and Tamar is a carefully placed break in the larger story. It shows what was happening in Judah’s family. Judah would later become an important leader. The story also shows the early stages of the family mixing with the people of the land. This helps explain why God sent the family to Egypt (chapters Genesis 39:39–47). 

The Egyptians kept themselves separate from other peoples (Genesis 43:32). Because of that, the Israelites were more likely to keep their own identity in Egypt than in Canaan.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: That Er was a wicked man is not surprising, since his mother was a Canaanite and his father a rebellious Israelite.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: This story describes the Lord as the sovereign judge who ended the lives of Judah's wicked sons.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
Perform your duty ... raise up offspring for your brother: This reflects the custom of levirate marriage (a practice where a man marries his dead brother’s wife).

In this custom, if a man died without children, his brother or nearest relative would marry the widow. The goal was to have a child who would carry on the dead man’s name and inherit his property. This practice was later included in God’s law for Israel (Deuteronomy 25:5–10). 

A close relative could refuse this duty, but he would be publicly shamed in the family for not preserving his brother’s name.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Onan married Tamar, but he was not willing to provide an heir for his brother. He had sexual relations with Tamar, but he did not fulfill his duty to his dead brother (Genesis 38:8).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Judah is now shown as the example for his sons' behavior. He also failed in his duty under levirate marriage toward Tamar, even though he was the next kinsman (see study note on 38:8). Judah and his sons acted too much like the Canaanites (see study note on 38:27–30; this contrasts with Boaz, who acted rightly in Ruth 3–4).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Without a marriage, the family's future was at risk. 

• Judah's wife … died: This made Judah available to fulfill the responsibility of providing an heir.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Tamar understood she needed to act to secure her family's future. Following the levirate custom (see study note on 38:8), she remained loyal to her dead husband. She had a legal right to have a child with Judah's son or Judah himself. So she tricked her father-in-law into having sexual relations with her. Again, Jacob’s family experiences deception, this time by a Canaanite daughter-in-law.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: It would be normal for Tamar to ask for a pledge if the man did not have the money to pay. A woman in such a position would not trust anyone to send the money.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: seal: A small cylinder made of stone or metal was carved with unique designs. People usually wore it on a cord around the neck. When it was rolled over soft clay or wax, it left a clear impression of the design.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Judah had gone to Tamar as a regular prostitute (Hebrew zonah, Genesis 38:15), whereas Hirah was mistakenly looking for a shrine prostitute (Hebrew qedeshah), of which there were none.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Judah acted hypocritically by condemning Tamar to death for adultery. When Tamar showed his seal, cord, and walking stick, it proved Judah was the father. He then withdrew the condemnation.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
She is more righteous than I: Judah admitted he had failed to provide an heir. It was wrong for Judah to visit a prostitute, but Tamar had a legal right to have Judah's child and acted on it. 

In the book of Ruth, the elders gave a similar blessing at the marriage of Boaz and Ruth. They prayed that God would make Ruth like Tamar (Ruth 4:12; compare Matthew 1:3, Matthew 1:5).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
Judah’s family line continued through Tamar. The twins replaced Judah’s two sons who had died (Genesis 38:7, Genesis 38:10). Their birth was similar to the birth of Jacob and Esau (Genesis 25:21–26). As with Jacob and Esau, the expected order of birth was reversed. In both cases, the twin connected with the color red (scarlet) did not remain in the first place.

In a similar way, Jacob gained the right to rule over his older brother (Genesis 27:29). This pattern seems to appear again in Judah’s family. The family line continued through Perez, not through the older son Shelah, whom Judah had tried hard to protect (Genesis 38:11; see 1 Chronicles 4:21), and not through the older twin Zerah (see Ruth 4:13–22; Matthew 1:3).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Perez moved ahead of his brother, just like Joseph would soon do with his own brothers (chapters Genesis 39:39–47).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Joseph was honest and faithful in his work for Potiphar. This is very different from Judah, who failed morally (chapter Genesis 38:38). God was with Joseph (Genesis 39:2–3, Genesis 39:21, Genesis 39:23). He helped Joseph succeed and become a blessing to others (see study notes on 12:1–9; 28:16–22), even while Joseph was a slave and later in prison.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Joseph began as a slave, alienated from his brothers and separated from his father; he ended as Pharaoh’s viceroy. Through the trips to Egypt, the covenant family went from the brink of apostasy, divided by jealousy and deception, to being reconciled and united by Judah’s intercession and Joseph’s forgiveness.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Apart from Genesis 38:7–10, this is the first time the story mentions God since Jacob built his altar in Bethel (Genesis 35:1–15). This is also the first time his covenant name, "the LORD," occurs since Jacob left Laban (Genesis 31:49).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: God began to bless Egypt through Joseph (see Genesis 22:18).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: A major theme in wisdom literature (wise teaching about how to live well; see study note on 37:2–50:26) is a warning to young people: sexual sin and other wrong behavior will lead to harm and ruin (compare Proverbs 5–7). Joseph resisted temptation because he had godly wisdom. He was guided by the fear of the Lord (a deep respect and reverence for God that leads to obedience; Proverbs 1:7; Proverbs 9:10).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: brought to us: Although Potiphar’s wife was speaking to slaves, she spoke to them as fellow Egyptians. She did this to make them support her and act as witnesses against the Hebrew man (a person from the people of Israel; see Genesis 43:32). This Hebrew man, Joseph, had gained Potiphar’s trust.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: This was the second time Joseph became imprisoned while faithfully doing the right thing. They deceptively used his clothing as false evidence (compare Genesis 37:23–24, Genesis 37:31–33).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Joseph thrived in prison because God was with him. Each time Joseph prospered, he was put in charge of something.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Joseph was so faithful and reliable that the captain of the guard trusted him with the care of two of Pharaoh’s officers.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Joseph did not lose faith in God’s promises, as evidenced by his readiness to interpret the dreams of two prisoners. He was still convinced that God’s revelation in his own two dreams (Genesis 37:5–11) was true, and he had not abandoned hope that they would be fulfilled. When the fellow prisoners’ dreams were fulfilled exactly as Joseph said, this confirmed that his previous dreams were from God.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Pharaoh’s cup-bearer and baker appeared worried because they sensed their futures were connected to these threatening and troubling dreams they could not understand. 

• Joseph still trusted that interpreting dreams was God's work. He knew he could understand them with God's help. He knew he had not misunderstood his own dreams.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Joseph listened to the dreams and gave their interpretations. These dreams were not trivial. They were serious warnings from God about what everyone would soon face. These two dreams also prepare for Pharaoh’s two dreams, which reveal the coming seasons of life and death that the nation would soon experience.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Because he knew that the chief cup-bearer was going back into Pharaoh’s personal service, Joseph saw an opportunity to seek his own release from prison.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The interpretations Joseph gave the prisoners proved true. The death of the chief baker speaks of the harsh realities of life in ancient Egypt, with a king whose word was his land’s highest law.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The chief cupbearer … did not remember Joseph: But God remembered him. Joseph's faith was about to be rewarded (chapter Genesis 41:41).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
Pharaoh's first dream was about cows. Cows often stood half-submerged in the Nile River's reeds to escape the heat and flies. They would leave the water to find grass. 

The second group of cows worried Pharaoh because they were thin but were able to swallow the fat cows.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
God had used two dreams to identify Joseph as a leader among his brothers (Genesis 37:5–11). He used two dreams to test Joseph’s faith in prison (Genesis 40:5–14). Now God used two more dreams to raise Joseph from prison to a place of high honor and authority.

Joseph had shown that he was faithful in small tasks. Now God would give him responsibility over greater things.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Pharaoh's second dream had a similar message. Seven shriveled heads of grain ate seven full heads of grain on one stalk and withered heads that grew afterward.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
The magicians and wise men were part of a group of people who claimed special skill in spiritual matters, such as understanding dreams and visions (see Exodus 8:18–19; Daniel 2:10–11). 

God used an Israelite slave to show that the wisdom of this world is limited (see Daniel 2). Even the most powerful nation is still under God’s rule and control (Daniel 2:20–23).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The chief cup-bearer finally remembered Joseph and testified that his interpretations were true.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Pharaoh quickly summoned Joseph from prison to explain his dreams. 

• Joseph shaved, following the Egyptian custom.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Joseph knew that only God could explain Pharaoh’s dreams (compare Genesis 40:8). He was sure God would reveal their meaning, as the dreams had a purpose (Genesis 41:25, Genesis 41:28).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Pharaoh recounted his dreams and testified that no human wisdom could interpret them.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Both dreams predicted that seven years of abundant crops would be followed by seven years of severe famine.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The two similar dreams showed that the matter has been decreed by God, and He will carry it out shortly. This was like the dreams of the two prisoners that God quickly fulfilled (Genesis 40:5–23). Joseph’s own two dreams (Genesis 37:5–11) were also about to come true (Genesis 41:37–46; Genesis 42:6–9).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• God’s message required a response. It was not given just to satisfy curiosity about the future. Joseph’s advice showed that he was wise and able to plan well. This is why Pharaoh chose him to lead (Genesis 41:37–40). 

• Joseph set up a system to store food. He placed one main leader over the work and local leaders in each area. He collected one-fifth (20 percent) of the grain and stored it for future needs. Later, wisdom literature (see study note on 37:2–50:26) teaches the same idea: plan for the future instead of living only for the present (see Proverbs 6:6–8; Proverbs 27:12).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
Pharaoh saw that Joseph was the right person for this work. He recognized that Joseph had the Spirit of God and was wise and understanding.

In this way, God showed his rule and authority over Egypt. Israelites who later read this story could trust that God would save them, just as he had promised.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Joseph was made the acting ruler or manager of Egypt.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Pharaoh’s signet ring had a seal used for signing documents. The seal was impressed in soft clay, which hardened and left a permanent impression of the ruler’s signature, which carried his authority. Numerous seals of this type have been found in archaeological digs. 

• The linen clothing and gold chain showed Joseph's new status as a ruler.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Pharaoh made Joseph second-in-command; all the people had to submit to him. Compare Psalm 105:16–22.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• As a sign of Joseph's new status, Pharaoh gave him an Egyptian name and a wife from an important family. 

• On was a center for sun worship and later came to be known as Heliopolis (meaning "sun city").

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Joseph was thirty years old: It had been about 13 years since his brothers sold Joseph into slavery (Genesis 37:2). 

• traveled throughout the land of Egypt: As a wise manager, his first priority was to understand his responsibilities.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Pharaoh's dreams were fulfilled just as Joseph had explained.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Despite his status and power, Joseph stayed true to his heritage. He gave his two sons Hebrew names. 

• Manasseh: Joseph's wealth and success helped him forget the pain of being away from his family. 

• Ephraim: By giving him this name, Joseph expressed his thanks to God for making him fruitful in Egypt.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Joseph’s wisdom paid off, for the seven years of plenty were followed by seven years of severe famine, but throughout Egypt there was plenty of food. Joseph had grain to sell to the Egyptians and to people from other countries as well.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Joseph did several unusual things to his brothers when they came looking for grain. The last time Joseph had been with them, they were filled with jealousy, hatred, and anger; they attempted to destroy their brother, and they deceived their father. Joseph put them through various tests, similar to the trying situations they had put him through, to see if they had changed.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: God used the famine to bring Israel to Egypt under Joseph’s rule, thus fulfilling two prophecies (Genesis 15:13; Genesis 37:7–11).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob may have believed that Benjamin would not be safe with his brothers.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Joseph's first dream (Genesis 37:5–11) was partially fulfilled when his brothers bowed down to him without recognizing him (see also Genesis 43:26; Genesis 44:14). It was totally fulfilled in Genesis 50:18. Joseph recognized his brothers immediately, but he could not reveal himself because he did not yet trust them to be the honest men they claimed to be (Genesis 42:10).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: they did not recognize him: This was because Joseph was now a grown man, not a boy. He did not have a beard, wore Egyptian clothes, and was in an unexpected position of power. He spoke to them through an interpreter (Genesis 42:23).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: You are spies!: The brothers thought Joseph was a spy for their father and treated him harshly (Genesis 37:2, Genesis 37:14, Genesis 37:18–28). Now, Joseph was testing them in a similar way to see their reaction.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Joseph knew that they had not always been the honest men they claimed to be.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Joseph put his brothers in prison for three days. He did this to see if they felt guilt for what they had done in the past (Genesis 42:21–23). The brothers had similarly thrown Joseph into a cistern-prison while they decided what to do with him (Genesis 37:24).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Rather than keep all but one, Joseph would release all but one to take grain home to their starving families.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
Surely we are being punished: The brothers believed that God was punishing them. They thought this because they now had to bring Benjamin to Egypt, even though their father did not want this. They connected this trouble with their past sin of selling Joseph to traders.

They began to see this as divine punishment (God judging wrong actions). The fear of divine punishment began to cause feelings of guilt that Joseph's cries for mercy and their father's tears had failed to produce (Genesis 37:34–35).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: you would not listen: Reuben had lost his place as leader (see study notes on 42:37; 49:3–4).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Joseph turned away from them and began to weep (compare Genesis 43:30; Genesis 45:2, Genesis 45:14; Genesis 50:1, Genesis 50:17). He might have heard a part of the story he had never known, like Reuben’s attempt to save him (Genesis 37:21–22, Genesis 37:29). Or, his brothers’ remorse might have moved him to forgive them.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: return each man’s silver to his sack: Joseph was testing his brothers. He wanted to appeal to their conscience (their inner sense of right and wrong) and make them face their past guilt. Once again, they were going home with silver instead of a brother (Genesis 37:28–35).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Joseph cared for his brothers' needs. He forgave them and provided for them (see study note on 42:24). God used Joseph's care to make the brothers more aware of their sin.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: What is this that God has done to us?: They realized God was responsible for everything happening, so they faced a day of reckoning for their sins.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The brothers’ report focused on the charge that they were spies and on the need to bring Benjamin back to Egypt with them. They did not mention that they were beginning to see God’s judgment (his just response to wrongdoing) for what they had done to Joseph.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Jacob was already grieving the loss of two sons and feared losing Benjamin if he went to Egypt. 

• You have deprived me of my sons: He did not know how true his words were. But these words probably troubled his sons' guilty consciences.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Reuben tried to take charge. He might have thought he could regain his father's favor (see Genesis 35:22). First, he hoped to rescue Joseph from death (Genesis 37:21–22, Genesis 37:29–30), and now by keeping Benjamin safe.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
Jacob continued to show special favor to Rachel’s only remaining son. He refused to let Benjamin go to Egypt, even if it meant that Simeon, Leah’s son, would not return.

Jacob’s deep grief later weighed heavily on the brothers’ conscience (Genesis 44:18–34).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: As the famine continued, Jacob's family needed more grain. But, they could not go back to Egypt without Benjamin (Genesis 42:16, Genesis 42:20). Jacob understood he was in a difficult situation. He needed more food but he would not risk losing Benjamin.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Judah solved the problem by taking responsibility for Benjamin’s safety. In this way, he succeeded where Reuben had failed. This change was important because Judah had earlier suggested selling Joseph to the Ishmaelites (Genesis 37:26–27) instead of killing him.
