Now he would secure Benjamin’s safety with his own life (see Genesis 44:18–34).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob provided everything he could to ensure a favorable reception from the Egyptian governor ("the man"; compare Genesis 32:13–21).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob finally trusted God Almighty with his family's future. This divine title emphasizes God's power (see also Genesis 17:1; Genesis 28:3; Genesis 35:11; Genesis 48:3; 1 Kings 19:10, 1 Kings 19:14; Revelation 21:22).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: When Joseph saw Benjamin with his brothers: Joseph knew Benjamin was well (see study note on 42:1–44:34). The feast was both a celebration and a test.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: the brothers were frightened: Compare Genesis 32:6–12. Their guilt stopped them from seeing that something good might happen.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The brothers, completely vulnerable and feeling the weight of God’s judgment on their consciences, approached the manager in desperation.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Joseph stopped being harsh to his brothers and treated them kindly instead.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: For the second time, the brothers bowed to the ground before him.This fulfilled his first dream (Genesis 37:7; see Genesis 42:6–7; compare Genesis 33:3).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: May God be gracious to you, my son: Joseph’s blessing to his full brother fulfilled Jacob’s prayer (Genesis 43:14).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• he was moved to tears for his brother: Compare Genesis 42:24. Joseph cried because of painful memories and lost years with his brother. He also felt joy and gratitude for seeing Benjamin again. 

• he went to a private room: This was because he was not ready to reveal his identity.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: in astonishment: This ruler knew more about the brothers than seemed possible (compare Genesis 44:15).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
The brothers experienced generous and gracious treatment from God through Joseph.

Joseph tested them. He showed special favor to Benjamin, who was also Rachel’s son. In the past, their father’s favoritism toward Joseph had caused jealousy and hatred.

By treating Benjamin with favor, Joseph tested whether they would respond with the same anger as before. This situation revealed whether their attitudes and behavior had changed.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The brothers seemed different. They felt sorry for what they did to Joseph. They showed honor by returning the money and by bringing Benjamin. Given a chance to get rid of Rachel’s other son, Benjamin, would they do it?

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Joseph was giving his brothers the chance to abandon Benjamin if they wanted to. Joseph was testing them to see if they were loyal to the family and faithful to their father.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• This description would help the brothers see that the ruler knew things that other people could not know.

• Hydromancy (trying to learn hidden things by pouring water into oil) and oenomancy (trying to learn hidden things by pouring wine into other liquids) were forms of divination (seeking knowledge through supernatural means) used in the ancient Near East. A special cup was often used for these practices.

Joseph was still pretending (see Genesis 42:7; compare Genesis 30:27; see also Leviticus 19:26; Numbers 23:23; Deuteronomy 18:10–11). He knew that only God reveals the future (see Genesis 37:5–9; Genesis 40:8; Genesis 41:16).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The brothers suggested a punishment that was too harsh. In ancient times, people often risked their lives based on their words. The palace manager agreed but imposed a punishment that matched Joseph's intentions (Genesis 44:17).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The palace manager knew where the cup was, but he created more anxiety by beginning with the oldest.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: they all tore their clothes: They knew what it would do to Jacob to lose Benjamin (Genesis 42:38).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: This time, the brothers did not bow politely (see Genesis 42:6–7; Genesis 43:26). They fell to the ground in desperation, fulfilling Joseph’s first dream for the third time (see Genesis 37:10).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Judah again spoke for the group. 

• God has exposed the iniquity of your servants: God was completing the work of repentance in their hearts. Judah again proposed that they all be punished. Benjamin was seemingly guilty of this theft, but all of the others were guilty of sin against Joseph. They preferred not returning to Jacob at all versus seeing his grief at the loss of Benjamin (Genesis 44:34).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Judah kept his promise to make sure Benjamin was safe (Genesis 43:8–10). His lengthy plea to take Benjamin's place in prison is one of the most sincere examples of intercession in the Bible (Genesis 44:33). It showed Judah's care for their father and his willingness to sacrifice everything for his brother. With this integrity, Judah proved himself a true leader, worthy of the firstborn's blessing (see John 15:13). Through him, Israel's kings would emerge (see Genesis 49:10). 

• The brothers had fully repented, as shown by Judah’s intercession. Because of their change, Joseph could reveal himself to them (Genesis 45:1–15). He arranged for the family to join him in Egypt, where there was food (Genesis 45:16; Genesis 47:12).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Judah was willing to give up his family, his future, and his freedom for others.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: In one of the book's most dramatic scenes, Joseph told his brothers who he was. This brought the process of reconciling with them to a climax (see also Genesis 50:14–21).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: This is the third time Joseph cried over his brothers in the story (see also Genesis 42:24; Genesis 43:30; Genesis 45:14; Genesis 50:17; compare Genesis 50:1).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The news shocked the brothers. They were unable to speak because of amazement and fear (Genesis 45:5; compare Genesis 50:15).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
it was not you who sent me here, but God: This is the main message of Jacob's family story (Genesis 37:2). As the Lord had told Abraham, he was bringing the Israelites into Egypt (Genesis 15:13). God sent Joseph ahead to prepare a way to save his family during the famine.

This is a clear statement about God’s sovereignty (his complete rule and control over all things). Joseph explained that God was at work through all events and human actions to carry out his plan.

Because God is in control, people can forgive and be restored to those who have hurt them. If people do not believe that God rules over all, they may blame others and try to get even. But those who trust God believe that he is at work, even through human evil (see also Romans 8:28–30).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Joseph told his brothers to inform Jacob. The entire family needed to move to Egypt and live in Goshen, a fertile area in the Nile delta (see Genesis 47:1–12). If they did not come to Egypt, they would not survive the upcoming five years of famine.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The region of Goshen was in the northeast corner of Egypt, a few days' walk from Canaan. Jacob's family stayed there because it had food and water for them and their animals. Later, the Egyptians forced them into slave labor there.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
Joseph was reunited with his brothers, first with Benjamin and then with the rest. Their previous hatred and jealousy of Joseph (Genesis 37:4–11) had come to an end. The brothers experienced forgiveness from God and from Joseph. Instead of commanding his brothers to bow down to him (see Genesis 42:6–7), Joseph welcomed them. Joseph held no grudge because he accepted what had happened as God’s work and saw the good that had resulted (see Genesis 50:14–21). 

This is how wisdom rules: The wise leader will forgive and restore (see study note on 37:2–50:26).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Joseph instructed his brothers to bring Jacob and the whole family to Egypt. Grateful for Joseph saving Egypt (Genesis 45:18; see Genesis 47:20), Pharaoh promised them the best land in Egypt. Joseph also gave them Egypt's finest products.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: This section marks a transition as the family moved from Canaan to Goshen, where they would live for the next 400years.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Do not quarrel on the way!: When they were away from Joseph, they might begin to accuse one another about the past or argue about how to explain what had happened to Jacob. It was now time to put the past behind them and enjoy the reunion.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: As expected, Jacob was shocked when he heard that his son Joseph was still alive and ruling all Egypt. But as he heard their full report and saw everything Joseph had sent, he became convinced it was true. At once, he prepared to go to Egypt and see Joseph again after 22 years.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
Jacob was revived: This royal invitation was a turning point for Jacob and his sons. Jacob was old and had little hope left. The 10 brothers were weighed down with guilt and fear.

This moment also fulfilled what God had said earlier (Genesis 15:13–16): his people would live in a foreign land for a time and there become a great nation, while remaining a distinct people.

The joyful news about Joseph changed the lives of this whole family for the better.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• set out: A little over 200 years earlier, Abraham also went to Egypt during a famine in Canaan (Genesis 12:10), and God protected him there. 

• Jacob first stopped at Beersheba, where Abraham had sacrificed and worshiped the Lord. This was after resolving land and water rights with the Philistines (Genesis 21:31–33). Isaac had lived there, and Jacob had lived there before fleeing from Esau’s anger (Genesis 28:10). 

• all that he had: See Genesis 46:5–7.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: God reassured Jacob about his move to Egypt.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: In a night vision, the Lord promised Jacob that he would be with him and make his family a great nation in Egypt. The same God who led them into Egypt promised to bring them back to live in Canaan.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: will close your eyes: He would have a peaceful death, surrounded by his family and many blessings from God (Genesis 49:33).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: This family history of Jacob's sons shows that all the tribes of Israel went to Egypt together. They would also leave together (see the book of Exodus).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: On: See study note on 41:45.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: numbered sixty-six persons: This includes those who traveled with Jacob to Egypt. But it does not include his sons' wives, the servants, or others in the household. It also does not include Joseph, Ephraim, Manasseh, and Jacob.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: seventy: This includes Joseph, Ephraim, Manasseh, and Jacob. Seventy is a symbolic number for perfection or completion (see “Symbolic Numbers” Theme Note). From these seventy (meaning all of Israel), the nation of Israel would grow and bless the seventy nations (meaning all the nations) of the world (see study note on Genesis 10:2–32; compare Genesis 12:3).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob was full of joy when he finally saw his son Joseph again.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: embraced him, and wept profusely: Joseph was 17 when he last saw his father (Genesis 37:2). Now, he was 39.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob was happy to see his beloved son alive. This son was the firstborn of his chosen wife Rachel and the designated family leader (see study note on 48:5–7; see also 1 Chronicles 5:1–2). This was more than a family reunion. It confirmed that God's plan was still in place.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The Canaanites would have mixed with the Israelites if they stayed in Canaan. But, Egyptians disliked Semitic shepherds due to ethnic pride and kept them separate (see Genesis 43:32). When Jacob’s family settled in Egypt, this separation helped them increase into a large nation while keeping their identity.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Ancient Egyptian texts do not mention Goshen (see study note on 45:10). Later Egyptian writings called it "the district of Rameses" (Genesis 47:11; see Exodus 1:11). It was fertile and near Joseph's court. This suggests it was on the eastern side of the Nile delta.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Pharaoh responded as Joseph hoped by giving Jacob’s family the best part of the land; he even gave some of the brothers oversight of his own livestock (Genesis 47:6).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: When Jacob entered and left Pharaoh’s court, he blessed Pharaoh. This showed Jacob's role as God's representative (see Hebrews 7:7). God promised to bless those who blessed Abraham’s family (Genesis 12:2–3), so Jacob blessed Pharaoh and Egypt.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The Lord blessed Pharaoh because Pharaoh was blessing Abraham’s descendants (Genesis 12:3). Through Joseph’s smart management in Egypt, the Lord saved the people from hunger and helped Pharaoh prosper. During the famine, Joseph sold food to the Egyptians, accepting money, livestock, and eventually land as payment. Then Pharaoh owned almost all of Egypt. Meanwhile, God gave Israel some of the best land in Egypt where they could live, work, and multiply.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: reduced the people to servitude: In Hebrew script, the words for slaves (Hebrew ‘abadim) and towns (Hebrew ‘arim) look very similar. Moving the people into the towns does not fit the context well, so most translations choose slaves as the reading that makes the most sense (compare Genesis 47:20).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: God blessed his people, just as he had promised Abraham. He said that Abraham’s descendants would be too many to count (Genesis 15:5; Genesis 22:17). But they still had to wait for the second part of the promise, that they would own the land of Canaan (Genesis 17:8).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• bury me with them: Compare Genesis 49:29–33. Jacob wanted to be buried with Abraham and Isaac in the cave of Machpelah (see study note on 49:29–33; see Genesis 23:1–20; Genesis 25:7–10; Genesis 35:27–29). 

• put your hand under my thigh: This custom was a serious oath to continue the covenant (compare with Genesis 24:1–9 and study note on 24:2). The covenant's main promise was descendants in the promised land that would be too many to count.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: After taking the oath, Jacob bowed in worship and thanked the Lord for making sure he would be buried with his ancestors in the promised land (compare 1 Kings 1:47).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: When Jacob blessed Ephraim and Manasseh, he showed faith in God's promise to continue. He understood that God's ways differ from human ways. From Jacob's long life, the writer of Hebrews chose the blessing of Joseph's sons as his greatest act of faith (Hebrews 11:21). Jacob followed God's will by giving the main blessing to the younger son instead of the older one, without any trickery or negative outcomes.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob remembered how God Almighty appeared to him and promised him Abraham's blessing: countless descendants living in the land … as an everlasting possession (compare Genesis 28:10–22).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob remembered Rachel (see Genesis 35:16–20) and blessed Joseph by making his two sons equal heirs with his other sons. The tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh would share equally with Jacob's other tribes (see Joshua 16–17). Jacob also gave Ephraim, Joseph’s younger son, the birthright (see 1 Chronicles 5:1–2). Because of this blessing, Ephraim and Manasseh became large and powerful tribes (see Joshua 17:14–18).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Like his father Isaac, Jacob now gave the blessing when his eyesight was failing (compare Genesis 27:1).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
The right hand was for the head of the firstborn, and Jacob was deliberately giving that position to the younger son. That pattern was followed for four consecutive generations: 

• Isaac over Ishmael, 

• Jacob over Esau, 

• Joseph over Reuben, and 

• Ephraim over Manasseh. 

Many years later, Ephraim became the leading tribe in the northern kingdom, superior to the tribe of Manasseh. The entire northern kingdom of Israel was occasionally called Ephraim (see study notes on 2 Chronicles 28:12; Isaiah 11:13; Ezekiel 37:15–28; Hosea 6:4; Zechariah 9:10).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
When Jacob blessed Joseph, he used three titles to describe the God he trusted: 

• the God who was in covenant with his fathers Abraham and Isaac (Genesis 28:13; Genesis 31:5, Genesis 31:42; Genesis 32:9; Genesis 46:3);

• the God who had been his shepherd (one who guides and cares for his people; see Genesis 49:24; Exodus 6:6; Psalm 23:1; Isaiah 59:20); and

• the angel (a messenger from God) who had rescued him from all harm.

Jacob prayed the same blessings for Joseph’s sons.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Not so, my father!: Joseph was upset because he expected God to act in a predictable way. But faith understands that God's ways and thoughts are different from human ones. Jacob spent his life learning this lesson, but he eventually understood and acted on it.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Joseph was later buried at Shechem as a sign that this extra portion of land belonged to him (Joshua 24:32). It seems that Jacob had conquered this area, though the event is not mentioned elsewhere.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob's words were carefully chosen prophecies. The days to come refer to the conquest and settlement of the promised land and the future messianic age. All tribes would share in the blessing and enter the land with Joshua. But they would not all participate in the same way.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
By faith, and as one who speaks for God, Jacob looked ahead to Israel’s future in the land and beyond to a greater future still.

At the end of the time of the patriarchs (the early fathers of Israel), he spoke about what would happen to each tribe. He did this as he considered each of his sons, one by one, just as Noah had done earlier (compare Genesis 9:25–27). 

The character and actions of each ancestor affected the lives of their descendants (Exodus 20:5–6; Exodus 34:6–7; Numbers 14:18; Jeremiah 32:18).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Uncontrolled as the waters: As the firstborn, Reuben should have led the family. But he acted without control, like water that boils or flows wildly (for example, Genesis 35:22). Because of this, Jacob said that Reuben would not succeed as a leader (see Genesis 37:21–22, Genesis 37:29; Genesis 42:22, Genesis 42:37–38; compare Judges 5:15–16; 1 Chronicles 5:1–2).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Simeon and Levi were violent and lawless. Instead of seeking justice, they allowed their uncontrolled anger to control them and ignored the value of life (Genesis 34:24–29). 

• I will disperse them: Simeon's land mostly became part of Judah's (Joshua 19:1, Joshua 19:9). Levi was given a more honorable future because the Levites became the priestly tribe (see Exodus 32:25–29). But they did not have their own region (Joshua 21).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The blessing for Judah is the most notable. In this message, Jacob said that Judah would be strong like a lion and would defeat his enemies. His brothers would also honor and praise him (compare Genesis 29:35; see, for example, Ruth 4:11–12; 1 Samuel 18:6–7; Psalms 2, Psalms 45:45, Psalms 72:72; Isaiah 11:1–13).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• This verse anticipates the kingship in Judah (compare Genesis 17:6, Genesis 17:16; Genesis 35:11). Although Joseph received the birthright blessing, Judah would provide Israel's rulers (see 1 Chronicles 5:1–2). Many kings from Judah would hold the scepter, the symbol of rule. The final king would be the one to whom the scepter belongs, the promised Messiah (see 2 Samuel 7:4–16; Psalms 2, Psalms 45:45, Psalms 60:60; Isaiah 11; Ezekiel 21:26–27; Zechariah 9:9; Revelation 5:5). 

• from between his feet: This is a poetic way to refer to reproductive organs. 

• until Shiloh comes and the allegiance of the nations is his: This wording reflects a long-standing way of understanding a difficult Hebrew phrase. Other translations include until the coming of the one to whom it belongs or until tribute is brought to him and the peoples obey. 

The right to rule Israel belongs to Judah’s descendant through David’s line (2 Samuel 7:8–16). He will eventually rule all nations, as shown by the bringing of tribute (see Psalms 68:29; Psalms 72:8–11; Isaiah 2:2–4; Ephesians 4:8–10).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• These descriptions describe the abundance of the Messiah’s kingdom (see Isaiah 61:6–7; Isaiah 65:21–25; Zechariah 3:10). When the Messiah arrives, the earth will be like paradise, full of beauty and abundance. 

• He ties his donkey to the vine: Grapevines will be so plentiful that people will use them as hitching posts, and wine will be as plentiful as fresh water (see Amos 9:13–14; Zechariah 3:10). 

• His eyes are darker than wine, and his teeth are whiter than milk: He will be strong and healthy, as will be the time of his rule. The miracle of turning water into wine was the first sign from Jesus that the Messiah had arrived (John 2:1–12). It was a preview of even better things to come.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The message said Zebulun would live by the sea and be a safe harbor. But when the land was divided, the tribe settled inland instead (see Joshua 19:10–16). The message did not give specific borders for the tribes.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Issachar would become a tribe that had to do hard work for others. Invading armies often controlled Issachar.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Dan (meaning "judge") was meant to bring justice. But the tribe chose betrayal, like a snake by the road, striking in a dangerous and unexpected way (see Judges 18).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: At this point, Jacob paused to speak words of hope. He may have been reminding his sons of their need to depend on the Lord. Or he may have been expressing hope in the Messiah’s reign, when he and his descendants would be rescued from all trouble, grief, and human betrayal.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Three of the six Hebrew words in this verse are wordplays on the name Gad, which means "attack." Gad will be attacked by raiding groups, but he will also attack them back. The tribes living east of the Jordan River often experienced raids on their borders (see Joshua 13; 2 Kings 10:32–33; 1 Chronicles 5:18–19).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Asher would be fertile and productive, providing rich foods. The tribe settled along the rich northern coast of Canaan.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Naphtali was like a doe. This may mean the tribe would live as a free people in the mountains (compare Judges 5:18). The tribe of Naphtali settled in the hill country northwest of the Sea of Galilee.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
This message about Joseph is longer and more detailed than the others, because it contains the main blessing(see 1 Chronicles 5:1–2). Jacob gave Joseph many promises of victory and success.

Some from the tribe of Ephraim who later won victories in battle include Joshua (Joshua 6, Joshua 8:8, Joshua 10:10, Joshua 12:12) and Deborah (Judges 4). From the tribe of Manasseh, Gideon (Judges 6–8) and Jephthah (Judges 11:1–12:7) were also victorious leaders.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: the Mighty One of Jacob … the Shepherd …the Rock of Israel … the God of your father … the Almighty: Five names for God introduce five blessings. God is the giver of all good things.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• The blessings from the heavens brought rain for crops. 

• The blessings of the depths below provided streams and wells. 

• The blessings of the breasts and womb led to many children.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Joseph … the prince of his brothers: He is a leader among his brothers, showing his strong character and high status.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The oracle about Benjamin describes a violent tribe (see Judges 20; 1 Samuel 9:1–2; 1 Samuel 19:10; 1 Samuel 22:17).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: These prophecies cover a wide range, predicting the future of various tribes in general terms. Individuals could receive great blessings from God through faith and obedience, no matter what happened to their clan.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
Bury me with my fathers: This grave in the land of Canaan represented hope for the future (compare Genesis 47:29–30). Others buried at the cave of Machpelah near Hebron were:

• Sarah (Genesis 23:19), 

• Abraham (Genesis 25:7–9), 

• Isaac (Genesis 35:27–29), 

• Rebekah, and 

• Leah.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
Jacob died at the age of 147 (Genesis 47:28), bringing his life of struggle and sorrow to an end. Jacob had always had a strong desire for God's blessing. He had a deep devotion and consistently relied on God no matter what happened. 

In the end, he died with genuine faith. He learned where true blessings come from. Through his faith, he would be able to pass these blessings on to his sons (Hebrews 11:21).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Like his father and his grandfather, Jacob’s death marked the end of an important time in Israel’s history.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Jacob’s body was embalmed for burial in typical Egyptian fashion. Embalming is the process of preserving a body after death.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The Egyptians mourned Jacob for 70 days, just two days less than they would for a pharaoh. This showed their great respect for Joseph.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
Joseph needed Pharaoh’s permission to leave his official duties for a short time. He wanted to bury his father in Canaan.

Pharaoh quickly gave permission to Joseph, who had once been a slave.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: This was Joseph’s first return to his homeland in 39 years. The trip was temporary. Hundreds of years later, the family of Israel would permanently leave Egypt, taking Joseph's bones with them for burial in the promised land (see Genesis 50:25).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: This journey to Canaan was a sorrowful one, because they went there to bury a man. The next journey into the land would be to live there.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: The brothers begged Joseph to forgive them, referring to themselves as his slaves (compare Genesis 37:7; Genesis 44:16, Genesis 44:33). They worried that Joseph had only made peace with them earlier because he wanted to see his father again. Now that Jacob and Pharaoh were not there to restrain him, they feared he might seek revenge. But Joseph wept because they still feared he would punish them.

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Joseph comforted his brothers, explaining that God intended to fulfill the promised blessing (compare Genesis 45:5, Genesis 45:7–9). He also promised them kindness and support (see Genesis 45:11).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: Joseph lived to see his great-great-grandchildren by Ephraim, and his great-grandchildren by Manasseh. This was a sign of God's blessing (see Psalm 128:6; Proverbs 17:6; Isaiah 53:10).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content: were brought up on Joseph’s knees: Placing them on his knees at their birth was a symbolic act signifying that they came from him and belonged to him (compare Job 3:12).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• God will surely visit you: These words from Joseph are repeated twice. They summarize the hope found in both the Old Testament and the New Testament. God would come to his people and act to save them.

God’s coming in the Messiah (the promised descendant of Abraham and God’s chosen king) would bring an end to the curse (the result of sin) and bring God’s promised blessing in a new creation (a renewed world). God’s faithful people would wait with hope for this to happen.

• Like his father, Joseph made his brothers promise to take his bones out of Egypt when God came to lead them back to Canaan ("attend to you"; see Exodus 13:19; Joshua 24:32; Hebrews 11:22).

entries.title: Genesis
entries.content:
• Joseph’s death signified the end of his generation (see study notes on 25:7–8; 35:1–29) and of the patriarchal age. From this point forward, God dealt with Israel as a nation. •

• Joseph’s body stayed in Egypt as a symbol of hope for slaves awaiting the promised land (see Exodus 13:19; Hebrews 11:39–40). They eventually buried him in Shechem (see Joshua 24:32), where Jacob had originally sent him (Genesis 37:13).
